To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Within this framework, our observations align with predictions made by models featuring a population of highly energetic sources concentrated primarily in the sky, and that include orientations influenced by the galaxy plane. This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in both angle and magnitude are evident across different centralities and become more pronounced in more central collisions and in collisions where the momentum of the particles is higher than 2 GeV/c. These findings, which have been compared to theoretical models such as iEBE-VISHNU, MUSIC, and AMPT, shed new light on the complex and not well understood initial conditions of these collisions. Furthermore, they highlight unique sensitivities to two crucial factors: the viscosity of quark--gluon plasma and the characteristics of the collisions' initial state. Given that these fluctuations tend to increase with the momentum of the particles, there is a need for re-examining existing theoretical models to gain a more precise and unbiased understanding of quark--gluon plasma's properties.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. A proposed network architecture known as DeepHMap++ integrates projection grouping and correspondence learning to attain optimal intermediate cues, thereby facilitating better-than-state-of-the-art results for difficult frontless cases. Furthermore, robust performance for front-facing scenarios is demonstrated through an straightforward adaptation of the proposed network, yielding results on par with top-tier baselines. Experimental evaluations were conducted utilizing the COFORD dataset, showing results for 60 tested models. The proposed methodology, effective for difficult frontless cases and easily extendable for front-facing scenarios, is suitable for real-world applications involving 6D object pose estimation. The code has been made publicly available at: https://github.com/lingyu-gh/DeepHMap++-baseline.

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 25% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps. All in all, this research highlights a range of numerical integrators commonly employed in biomolecular simulations, including the Verlet and Langevin integrators, and proposes an alternative method that was found to outperform these integrators in resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations. Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. This new algorithm first determines the marginal contribution of each layer's centrality values, followed by a iterative adjustment of the values using a weighted average of the layers. We demonstrate how our method can be applied to real-world datasets, including a prominent example from the field of academia where researchers collaborate across different disciplines. Our results show that our method effectively identifies the most crucial nodes that bridge different layers and our algorithm's efficiency makes it suitable for large networks. We also explore how our approach can be expanded to include weighted networks and find that the most influential nodes are generally robust against different parameters and distributions of degrees and weights. We conclude by discussing potential applications and future developments of our method. We have made our code available to the public.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. A comprehensive discussion on existing and new results is presented in the study. A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. We also explore the condition under which states generated by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers are equivalent, and discover that this condition is linked to the average photon number of the coherent state involved in the catalytic process. Consequently, we establish that over a particular range, states produced by these two devices are indistinguishable, as they exhibit identical statistical distributions. Furthermore, our investigation enables the identification of a specific regime in which the quantum states generated by these two devices can be interchanged, thereby offering a means of 'quantum state conversion'. We propose an experimental setup for generating SPCCSs using linear optical elements, as well as a successive detection scheme that complements the catalytic process. This setup facilitates the direct measurement of various non-classical properties of these states, as well as the distribution of the detected photons. We also analyze the relationship between the statistical distributions of the detected photons and the initial coherent state parameters, as well as the quantum-optical catalytic device used. These findings provide valuable insights into the non-classical properties of SPCCSs, as well as the distribution of the detected photons, and enable the identification of specific regimes associated with quantum state conversion. We further investigate the scenario in which the coherent state input to the catalytic process is generated using a different beam splitter, as well as the associated condition under which the resulting SPCCSs exhibit the same statistical distributions. We discover that this condition is linked to the precise configuration of the beam splitter used to generate the coherent state, as well as the average photon number involved in the catalytic process. Consequently, our investigation enables the validation of the quantum state conversion capability of SPCCS

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs a patch-based input to accommodate varied sizes of esophageal segments and incorporates residual connections to simplify the network. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied feeding tube configurations and incorporated air-filled segments as part of the training data to account for possible proximal air pockets. Our model produced a precision of 0.89, a recall of 0.84, and a F-score of 0.86 when compared to the reference standard provided by human experts. These results indicate that a purely CT-based approach can effectively and efficiently identify and outline tumors in the esophagus. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation.

Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. To tackle these challenges, we highlight opportunities for innovative techniques, such as exploiting non-parallel data, leveraging monolingual Hindi resources, and exploring more effective hate speech detection methods. By addressing these issues, we believe NLP researchers and developers can make a more significant impact to benefit multilingual communities worldwide.

High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. I discuss feasible routes to evaluating systems using smaller, more manageable datasets, including aggregating existing human-generated descriptions, descriptions produced by automatic systems, and pseudoreference data generated by these systems. I also explore the possibility of using pseudoreference data to engage blind users in description generation, enabling more efficient use of their expertise. Tantalum oxide compounds, with the formula Ta$_2$O$_5$, are distinguished by unique properties including high dielectric values and minimal reflectivity. Recent studies have also considered Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanoparticles as potential enhancers for hadron therapy treatments of cancer. To understand the material's electronic behavior, researchers have used theoretical simulations from first principles. Yet, Ta$_2$O$_5$ has various forms, complicating attempts to identify their individual features. To resolve this issue, researchers used time-dependent density functional methods to study the energy loss function in Ta$_2$O$_5$, specifically in its optical state, and across different polymorphs. These studies have demonstrated that experimental reflection loss signals can be overinterpreted, leading to incorrect conclusions about Ta$_2$O$_5$'s energy gaps and electronic structures. On the other hand, researchers found that both experimental and theoretical energy loss spectra in Ta$_2$O$_5$ exhibit similar shapes, and that the material's dielectric value primarily relies on its local electronic structures rather than crystal structure. To further investigate Ta$_2$O$_5$'s local structure and potential bonding lengths, researchers used Monte Carlo methods to compare and distinguish between various Ta$_2$O$_5$ polymorphs based on reflection loss spectra alone. To validate these results, researchers used X-ray scattering experiments to analyze the local structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ polymorphs, and found that both experimental and theoretical approaches yielded identical results, indicating that the ground state crystal structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ is $\alpha$-Ta$_2$O$_5$. This conclusion has been supported by multiple lines of evidence from experimental and theoretical studies. Despite being an insulating material, researchers have also demonstrated that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s energy loss spectra can be understood using time-dependent density functional methods, providing a more comprehensive explanation for its unique energy gaps and dielectric values. To conclude, this study has demonstrated that Ta$_2$O$_5$'s energy gaps and dielectric values primarily rely on local electronic structures rather than crystal structure, and that researchers should exercise caution when interpreting reflection loss signals and comparing them to experimental results. Additionally, this study has identified the ground state crystal structure of Ta$_2$O$_5$ as $\alpha$-Ta$_2$O$_5$, and has provided a more accurate explanation for the material's unique energy gaps and dielectric values. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas where residents are less diligent in nature, and cultures place little emphasis on adherence to norms, we found increased circulation of all news, including credible sources. Additionally, we observed a "supply" response to demand, as users in areas with higher demand for misinformation engaged more with news sources known to circulate false information. These findings highlight the significance of The Big Sort in understanding online misinformation dissemination and suggest that reducing population size or increasing user diligence and norm adherence in those areas may help mitigate this issue. Moreover, interventions targeting user behavior and culture could be more effective than measures focusing solely on platform features or broad societal changes. Lastly, our research highlights the value of integrating geographical perspectives with personal and social media influences in analyzing online misinformation dissemination. The study's findings have implications for strategies aimed at reducing misinformation dissemination and circulating reliable information in these communities. The findings can be applied to similar online forums in the United States and provide a research methodology for other domains involving combined analysis of theoretical and online data. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. The proposed approach also yields a notably lower generalization error when compared to a range of single-domain and CDR models, as validated through a thorough hyperparameter tuning process. The code for MSDCR is publicly available at: https://github.com/lingyu-gh/MSDCR.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. The proposed method the paper's associated repository provides additional details on Hypatia's implementation, available at https://github.com/HypatiaOpt/Hypatia.jl. The repository also includes a list of previously processed test cases and reference solving times. The development of Hypatia is ongoing, and researchers and practitioners are invited to contribute new cone definitions and formulations. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. Our study highlighted the challenges of effective generalization in MRIQC through the incorporation of explicit population factors in modeling, suggesting future research opportunities in this domain. Moreover, we made available our analysis of the CATI dataset in conjunction with publicly accessible resources, including MRIQC, brain age estimates, and metadata. This combines metadata and computational outcomes from a large quantity of participants, boasting over 9,000 recorded assessments of MRI data quality. To understand how private electric vehicles influence the recovery of power grids following outages, we developed a mathematical framework that incorporates decentralized decision-making in both transportation and energy systems. We utilized multi-agent optimization to model this process and overcame computational challenges through an efficient algorithm based on precise reformation. Numerical analysis was conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding valuable policy insights and paving the way for further study into grid resilience with private EVs within interconnected transportation and energy networks. Ultimately, our research provides a foundation for exploring various management strategies and their implications on grid resilience, transportation, and energy consumption.

We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Consequently, this research provides the first instance of a study on a multi-agent system exhibiting rendezvous behavior utilizing the Motivation Dynamics model. This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Furthermore, we explored the phase stability and energy of different structures for these materials, and suggested possible synthesis methods for the CmSn3 compound. Lastly, we examined the misfit layer structure of the GdxCm1-xSn3 compound consisting of alternate GdSn3 and CmSn3 layers, and found that it favors a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and has a relatively small lattice mismatch of 1.14%. This compound also demonstrates good mechanical stability and robust magnetic properties. Consequently, we propose the GdxCm1-xSn3 series with the misfit layer structure as an alternative to exchange coupled composite materials. Lastly, our findings are applicable to related compounds in the LnSn3 and AnSn3 families. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn. Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. Greater precision in measuring galactic halo properties and a more refined calculation of lens-induced scattering are also necessary for further improving this estimator. Ultimately, this research highlights a previously underutilized SN Ia data resource and suggests that a more comprehensive investigation is necessary to encompass effects of strong lensing, double lensing, and gravitational magnification by foreground structures. The proposed estimator can be applied to current and upcoming SN Ia datasets, including the SH0ES2 and LSST surveys. The calculable magnification scatter offers additional insights into the underlying physics of the observed cosmological parameters and can be used as a prior for future analyses. The anticipated precision of measuring galactic halo properties will decrease at $z \approx 1.5$, and the impact of lens-induced scattering on SN Ia cosmology will become more substantial in the foreseeable future. The calculable lens-induced scattering effect on SN Ia distances moduli will persist at $z \approx 3$ and becomes a dominant component of the measurement error at $z \approx 4$. The research suggests that targeted surveys for double lensing by foreground structures and strong lensing by foreground structures and gravitational magnification by foreground structures and background structures are feasible and necessary. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, we discovered that dense T center arrays within the device layer enable the creation of high T center densities near the interface simply by adjusting the ion implantation dose, and that these densities can reach ~10^18 cm^-3, surpassing the projected amount required for quantum repeatable read-out. Additionally, we investigated the effects of heat treatment and oxidation on T center densities and bond configurations, and found that heat treatment and mild oxidation increase the fidelity of read-out, while more intense oxidation reduces the fidelity due to bond configuration alterations and increased spectral diffusion. And finally, we found evidence of a previously unknown silicon defect center, which we call the Si-C center, and which has a similar absorption feature to the T center but with a distinct emission spectrum and different optical transition behavior. And so, we were able to create a device-based model of this new defect center, and discovered that it shares some similarities with the T center, the GeH4 center, and the SiF3 center, and that it has a more extensive and richer spectral signature than the T center. And so, we believe that further investigation of this new defect center will be crucial for better understanding silicon quantum technologies. And so, we have made all of our device-based simulation code available publicly, in the hope that it will be useful for other researchers who are investigating this new defect center and silicon quantum technologies in general. And so, we have also proposed a method for further increasing the fidelity of read-out on the T center by optimizing the device layer depth, and we have shown that this will require the development of new SOI wafer fabrication techniques that allow for precise control over the device layer depth. Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Unlike the general linear group, the conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K) cannot be categorized based on the number of missing integers in the set {0, 1,..., n}. Instead, this distinction highlights the significance of a particular property of the trace matrix, which arises when examining the transformation of a polynomial under a specific transformation of its variables. This property ultimately leads to the concept of a particular subset of the collection of non-negative integers (represented as a string of integers) that is arranged in descending order and from which a set of integers has been removed. Given two strings of integers, they are considered equivalent if they differ by some permutation, in other words, they represent the same ordered set of integers. As an example, the string (4, 3, 2, 0) is equivalent to (0, 2, 3, 4). Additionally, given a string of integers (n-1, n-3, n-4,..., 1 or 0), if it contains an odd number of integers then it is impossible to derive any information from it, but if it contains an even number of integers then it can be further categorized based on whether the last integer is 0 or not. Furthermore, considering two fields K1 and K2, if Sp_n(K1) and Sp_n(K2) share the same conjugacy classes then their polynomial rings must be isomorphic, but this does not imply that the fields themselves are isomorphic. This condition is only met if the field K has a finite number of conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K). A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. We also explore various levels of incompatibility to demonstrate how it affects the value function and the optimal acceptance criterion. Our results can be valuable to clinicians and patients in making informed decisions about kidney transplants. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our study also explores the practical utility of these models, leveraging the similarity of company names as a proxy for operational mergers and acquisitions, and the polarity of financial terms to understand the temporal dynamics of sentiment in the market. Our work highlights the limitations of these models, suggesting that the ease with which they are applied has been mismatched with the complexity of the problem. Our results are made available through an interactive online dashboard at https://www.paritosh.com/research/w2v_polarities. Our research highlights the challenges of interpreting these models, the difficulty of separating semantic from co-occurring distributions, and the necessity of adopting more sophisticated methods that consider the generative processes of these models, along with the need for caution when applying these models to domains like finance. Our findings are expected to guide both practitioners and researchers in their use and development of these models. Our research is focused on the word2vec model but our results are likely to be applicable to other NLP embeddings such as the GloVe model. This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. Furthermore, we've compared our results to existing literature, demonstrating good agreement and highlighting the advantages of our hybrid method. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research is further distinguished by the inclusion of an algorithm tailored to the scenario involving multiple agents when action costs are fixed, in addition to general multiplayer games setting. Existing results on learning rationalizable actions without considering swap-regret as a controlling factor are also leveraged to extend our findings to the realm of (swap-)Follower equilibria, an previously unexplored area. This work is accompanied by a corresponding sample lower bound, demonstrating that the proposed learning framework for a specific scenario is attainable with a sample complexity that matches the designated benchmark. The development of an efficient algorithm to learn CE when the sample lower bound indicates a transition to an exponentially dominated region is challenging. This research fills this void by developing an innovative approach called the Exponential Gap algorithm, which achieves a polynomial sample complexity in the exponential gap dimension. This achievement is further validated through an associated sample lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. The developed framework is also applicable to the challenging scenario of learning CE in multiplayer games with an unknown transition distribution, a setting that has not been previously addressed. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. In this paper, we outline our theory pipeline's capabilities for simplifying this process and outline an open-source code called Theory Pipeline Format Converter (TPFC). TPFC addresses the formatting incompatibilities between PDF fitting codes and various theoretical predictions, including calculations of scattering cross-sections and particle decays. We also discuss the process of aligning the scales employed in different processes and predictions. In addition to code known as Joust, developed by the Monte Carlo event generator Sherpa, TPFC includes an interface named Theory I/O which allows users to utilize TPFC's features. We demonstrate TPFC's utility by converting the predictions of the Monte Carlo event generator Monte Carlo Tools for Les Houches Events (MTTOLE) into the format suitable for PDF fitting codes. MTTOLE is an extension of the code Monte Carlo Tools for Les Houches Events (MTTOLE) developed by the Monte Carlo event generator Monte Carlo Tools for Les Houches Events (Monte Carlo Tools for Les Houchen Events). Standard experience replay enables agents to retain information from prior iterations. However, the current approach equally values all collected observations, neglecting their varying significance. This approach prioritizes past observations more likely to represent the current target distribution. We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We observe that in the limit where the discrete version of the models approaches their continuous equivalents, the domains converge to the upper half-plane and the first orthant, respectively, with the associated Gaussian free fields converging to zero. Additionally, we establish that the imaginary surfaces induced by stochastic geometric constructions equidistant from a line segment are paired with the associated Gaussian free fields. This pairing provides a natural ordering of the points on the line segment. We use this ordering to demonstrate that the end-point of a multiple SLE evolving in the upper half-plane with the real axis as its boundary is not almost surely the rightmost point. This result holds for a wide range of parameters including those typically used in physical and biological applications. Consequently, we can couple multiple SLE evolving in the upper half-plane and the first orthant with the real and positive reals as their boundaries with the Dyson and Bru-Wishart models respectively. Ultimately, this pairing yields domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. This coupling is more versatile than the usual one based on the Brownian loop soup. It extends to time-changing branches of the SLE$_\kappa$ for $\kappa\in (0,8)$. Furthermore, it provides a natural ordering of the points on the line segment, which can be achieved by considering the time-evolving branch of the SLE$_\kappa$ with the boundary at the real axis. This ordering is equivalent to the order induced by the harmonic layer associated with the branch, which in turn is equivalent to the order induced by the Imaginary Surface. This equivalence allows us to order the marked points on the line segment according to the depth of the points in the harmonic layer, which is directly related to the length of the associated branch of the SLE$_\kappa$. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. Understanding how genomic elements affect specific traits through genome-wide association studies remains complex due to the sheer number of available annotations. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. This approach can incorporate multiple annotation types and has been successfully applied to eighteen human traits such as blood, platelet counts, metabolism-related disorders, height, obesity and a bowel disease, by examining 450 distinct genomic features across one hundred plus tissues and cells types. Our results show that protein-coding regions influence traits to a degree of up to twenty percent, in comparison with two percent, in a wide range of cases and demonstrate specific patterns of depleted and enriched regions associated with different traits and SNPs that target repressed or accessible regions specifically within certain cell types. Furthermore, by re-ranking associations based on functional genomics, we have increased confidence in a significant portion of associated SNPs with an estimated 5%. Additionally, our approach has been applied to identify potential indirect effects of DNA accessibility, with an estimated 10% of associated SNPs showing this type of interaction. Our method and findings are available online at http://geneanc.igb.illinois.edu/. Our study highlights the vast impact of non-coding genomic elements on trait-associated SNPs and shows that a significant portion of associated SNPs are direct or indirect effects of changes in specific cell types, tissues or the genome as a whole. By applying this approach to different traits and cell types, we have shown the widespread influence of DNA accessibility, repression and mutation tolerance on associated SNPs and provided tools and insights that can be used to better understand and analyze a wide range of complex traits and conditions.

Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. These findings have significant implications for the estimated number of radio pulsars and neutron star binaries within the galaxy. Furthermore, to match the observed population of X-ray binaries at the Milky Way's center, involving a neutron star as the primary component, with outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade, the theory suggests that at least half of the known variables remain inactive, and the estimated number of radio pulsars and neutron star binaries within the galaxy could be twice the previously estimated figures. By drawing a comparison to classical mechanics, where circular motion generates Coriolis and centrifugal forces, analogous effects arise, specifically spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, and the interplay of these forces with the spin-orbit and the redshift of energy levels. These effects can persist for a few picoseconds following the initial stimulation, and potentially amplifying their magnitude could make this approach a promising means of controlling localized quantum states and chemical reaction barriers via vibration. This framework also provides a framework for understanding and manipulating static and dynamic effects of spin-rotation coupling and the centrifugal field in both molecules and crystals. This approach could further integrate with other driving forces, such as strong magnetic fields, light, and temperature, potentially leading to novel phenomena like the analogs of the centrifugal field effect on the superconducting gap, the centrifugal Meissner effect, and the centrifugal Doppler effect. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through an iterative procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which, in comparison to standard generation methods, results in an average 137% improvement in NLI Diversity. Moreover, this method was integrated into a state-of-the-art conversational agent, which, in evaluation tests, yielded a 25% increase in NLI Diversity and achieved high scores on other evaluation metrics. The code for this research has been made publically available at https://github.com/PranavTyagi/NLI_Diversity.

Bipartite graphs depicting connections between distinct groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. The task of reducing edge crossings within these visualizations can be computationally intensive, yet might not always guarantee sufficiently low crossings levels to maintain the visualization's clarity. In contrast, an approach has been developed to remove edge crossings by splitting specific nodes, targeting the minimum number required to yield an edge-free (planar) drawing. The question of determining if an edge-free representation exists after breaking at most a specified number of nodes remains tractable in relation to that number. The paper presents an algorithm capable of efficiently solve this problem for a given integer $k$, by breaking a maximum of $k$ nodes, within a time framework proportional to $O(2^k \cdot poly(n))$, where $n$ represents the total number of nodes across the graph. The development of this algorithm also leads to a more advanced result, the inclusion of a parameter that represents the maximum desired node degree, enabling the development of a bipartite graph from scratch, as well as the validity of a variety of existing models that restrict node degrees, such as circular and bipartite drawings restricted to non-crossing curves. The approach discussed here is based on a new form of 2-tiered graph representation that can be manipulated by splitting nodes, and includes a method to determine if a node can be safely excluded, as well as a procedure to search exhaustively through all possible distributions of nodes following the specified splitting criteria. The development of the algorithm also involves a number of subroutines, each with a separate application, and capable of being combined with other existing methods such as the hybrid method of Bouchard and Tamura, as well as the clean-inflation method, among others. The general approach discussed here can be applied to a wide range of problems related to bipartite graph representations, such as the recognition of specific graph types, as well as the validation of models that restrict node degrees in general and circular bipartite drawings specifically. The algorithm developed here is also capable of handling large-scale instances of these problems, as demonstrated by the testing of the algorithm on a variety of real-world datasets. The paper concludes by identifying a number of open problems and possible directions for future research, such as the investigation of a number of special cases, as well as the development of methods to reduce the size of the search space

A localized alteration in knot diagrams is referred to as an unknotting operation. It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory; they serve a purpose in analyzing the intricacy of knots and knot-related properties. Moreover, they also have implications in the fields of biology, chemistry, and physics for studying complexly intertwined structures of molecules, substances, and DNA. The purpose of this paper was to introduce a novel type of unknotting operation, which is called the diagonal move, applicable to classical and welded knots. The study shows that the cross-over change, the delta-move, the sharp-move, the gamma-move, the n-gon move, the pass move, and the 4-move can be achieved by applying a sequence of diagonal moves. The study also delves into defining a distance measure that originates from the diagonal move, as well as examining its characteristics. The investigation concludes by demonstrating that the newly introduced distance measure is identical to the number of variations in diagram configuration, which is referred to as the 1-distance. The term 1-distance was initially introduced by Kauffman and Vogt in 2006. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived. Furthermore, a critical threshold is identified, beyond which increasing the degree of the network does not significantly reduce the size distribution of the removed components. Additionally, a critical period is determined during which changes in network degree primarily influence the distribution of removed components rather than their size. This micro-level analysis provides a more precise understanding of network dynamics and can be applied to various networks, as demonstrated by examining a regular graph. This study also sheds light on the differences in distribution sizes resulting from random attacks versus targeted attacks. Finally, the findings can be applied to other networks, as demonstrated by examining a random attack on a scale-free network. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors. Although this topology has been theoretically assessed, its practical implementation is complicated by the stringent requirements for high precision in constructing the detector components. A simplified variant of the design is also presented as a more feasible alternative. The challenges of implementing this design are discussed, along with potential solutions and future research directions. The theoretical analysis has been supplemented with numerical simulations based on real detector parameters, offering a tangible pathway to overcoming the limitations of advanced gravitational wave detectors. The sloshing Sagnac topology may also be applicable to other interferometric systems used in spectroscopy and sensing applications. The code used for simulations is publicly available on GitHub at the specified URL. The design's potential for improving sensitivity could be further optimized by incorporating material engineering advancements that minimize optical loss and enhance the coupling between the detector's components. The proposed topology has the potential to break through the threshold of detecting big binary neutron star mergers of low mass and offers valuable lessons for designing and analyzing other interferometric systems. Recent large-scale MIMO systems are considered an exciting development, capable of providing rapid data transfer in crowded environments. As a result of their substantial size, MIMO arrays are subject to space-based disruptions and varying ranges that affect how data is perceived by nearby devices. With a high number of devices often present in applications for these systems and the scarcity of pilot signals available for them, designing protocols and scheduling algorithms is increasingly complex. To address this challenge, a new joint protocol has been developed that leverages varying reception areas of devices for better access and prioritizes the scheduling of devices with distinct reception areas for more efficient signal sharing. According to the results obtained, the newly designed protocol delivers considerable gains over traditional approaches in terms of overall connectivity, reduces space-based interference, and significantly boosts the number of active devices in scenarios with dense arrays. The developed scheme also delivers a 25% reduction in the system's signal-to-noise ratio required for reliable communication. The newly designed protocol was tested in an open environment with a range of scenarios, including scenarios with crowded conditions near buildings, inside buildings, and around corners, and showed it to be highly effective in such situations. The newly developed protocol was also found to be highly compatible with various CIO configurations, including configurations with arrays that are closely packed, moderately packed, and sparsely packed, and delivered performance gains in all these scenarios. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Moreover, it highlights the risk of storage units contributing to market instability and extreme price fluctuations. Active learning algorithms effectively achieve this by pinpointing data samples that are essential for improving DNN performance. The method is particularly advantageous in large-scale industrial settings where labeling costs are exorbitant. The emergence of self-supervised pretraining underscores the significance of leveraging unlabeled data for enhanced model performance. Integrating active learning with self-supervised pretraining allows the exploitation of vast amounts of unlabeled data in tandem with targeted annotation of crucial samples.

Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. This model incorporates a reservoir formed by heavy holes and exhibits behavior similar to that observed in the actual HgTe samples. By comparing theoretical predictions with experimental data, our findings also demonstrated the presence of a reservoir formed by heavy holes in HgTe quantum wells, exceeding the critical thickness of 3.5 nm, although more examination is required to thoroughly validate this conclusion. This study examines transport phenomena in HgTe quantum wells within the Dirac regime and provides a comprehensive understanding of the underlying physics. This knowledge can be applied to other materials featuring a Dirac cone and edge states, and it also paves the way for examining interaction between a single edge state and a massive reservoir in a mesoscopic setup. Furthermore, we propose a possible modification of the setup that would involve coupling a single edge state to a massive reservoir in a self-consistent way, examining the impact of this interaction on the edge state, and analyzing the resulting zero-bias kinks on quantized resistance platesaus. This interaction causes a shift in the neutral point, resistance oscillation plateaus, and zero-bias kinks that resemble the results obtained in actual HgTe samples, although more examination is required to validate these conclusions. This examination requires developing a more comprehensive model that takes into account the specific details of the HgTe material, heavy-hole Landau levels, and edge-state interaction, which can be examined through a variety of experimental techniques, including real-space imaging, magnetotransmission spectroscopy, and quantum transport measurements. This examination can provide a more complete understanding of the behavior of heavy-hole Landau levels within the gapless HgTe regime, which can be applied to other materials featuring a Dirac cone and edge states. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Additionally, we've analyzed the worst-case scenario where our model fails to converge, finding an upper bound on the number of scheduling modes that affects convergence. Furthermore, we've validated the accuracy of our payoff estimation method, showing our approach matches a more complex estimation method made possible by simulation due to computational constraints. In a scenario with a single cell and variable distance between cells, our model fails to converge when the distance falls below a certain threshold, while in a real-world scenario with a single small cell inside a large macrocell, our solution successfully manages interference, even when the worst-case number of scheduling modes is applied. In both cases, our solution reduces unnecessary time spent on scheduling, leading to increased system throughput. Lastly, we've explored alternative payoff estimation methods, finding that our current approach already utilizes the most accurate estimation possible, while also proposing a more complex estimation method that could be applied to other challenging games. Lastly, we conclude by outlining potential directions for further research, including incorporating user prioritization and dynamic changes in cell traffic conditions.

In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which acquires an understanding of gradients. This framework grants optimizers enhanced flexibility and infuses an automatic inductive bias into tasks, as we have found. Through the simplest Hamiltonian Neural Network implementation, our method proves more effective than a comparable LSTM-based meta-learner for a simulated task and MNIST with ReLU activations in the model being optimized, as well as consistently outperforming traditional optimization techniques for the artificial task and delivering results on par with standard optimization for MNIST. Nonetheless, we have observed difficulties in applying our method to more complicated models, highlighting the challenges of its current iteration. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghalegh.AMPL.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Furthermore, the proposed system demonstrates significant advantages over alternative methods of model augmentation and scoring techniques. These findings support the potential of a human-in-the-loop online multi-agent approach in enhancing the reliability of machine learning models, making this proposed system a valuable addition to the field. The proposed system's versatility also presents potential applications in areas beyond critical situations, such as in tasks involving artificial intelligence agents that interact with humans. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Lastly, $J_n^T$ can be identified as the normalized colored volume of both a specific virtual link and a biperiodic link, implying that the volume conjecture holds true for these links. The investigation also yields an formula for a specific non-virtual link, referred to as the complete toroidal volume link, which is distinguished from its virtual counterparts by its volume, and whose polynomial is expressible through a product of two tridiagonal polynomials. The study of $J_n^T$ also yields an intrinsic definition of the tridiagonal Riemann surface invariants introduced in a prior study, as well as an infinite family of tridiagonal polynomials associated with the volume conjecture, whose members include both known and newly defined polynomials, such as the modified truncated colored Jones polynomial, the toroidal colored Jones polynomial of a link complement, and the volume of a link in a thickened torus. A novel approach utilizing hypernyms' definitions and context-gloss augmentation is presented, which achieves the best results according to both manual and automated evaluation metrics. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. This finding was also used to calculate the ratio of proton-proton to proton-lead cross sections, with a value of 0.93 ± 0.09, and demonstrated that the CMS detector could successfully operate in the high-radiation environment of heavy-ion experiments. The discovery paved the way for exploring rare processes like top quark production and same-sign top quark pairs in future lead-lead collisions. The underlying event in these events was found to be comparable to that in proton-proton collisions at a similar energy, and the data set allowed for initial studies of nuclear modification factors and forward-central rapidity gaps. The measured cross section for top quark production in proton-lead collisions at this energy exceeded the expected background by more than 15 standard deviations, a record at the time of achievement. The finding was significant because it opened up possibilities for studying the interaction between quarks and gluons at the level of individual nucleons within heavy-ion collisions, and it marked the first time that the top quark had been detected in collisions involving an atomic nucleus. The discovery of the top quark in proton-nucleus collisions also marked a milestone in the development of the CMS experiment, demonstrating that it could operate effectively in the intense radiation environment of heavy-ion experiments and facilitating future research on the experiment's ability to safely operate in heavy-ion collisions.
