This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement. Moreover, our proposed framework effectively handles schema and value filling when database contents are accessible, with performance indicators showing significant gains over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy. Code is available at github.com/ASU-HanWang/End2EndCDTSQL.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of universally accepted DP formulation in graph-based contexts. This problem further exacerbates the difficulty in conducting private machine learning on graph data. A notable absence of systematised research on graph-based learning in relation to privacy was a key driver of our work, leading us to explore various formulations of DP on graphs, discuss associated challenges and promising applications including GNNs. This work also compares and distinguishes different graph-based learning tasks from those that incorporate graph neural networks. Ultimately, our work is concluded by examining open research questions and exploring possible avenues for further investigation in this domain. This work is part of the ongoing effort #PaCC: Privacy Accelerated Computing Consortium.

Building upon this description, we derived a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic model that simulates long-lasting non-equilibrium situations while sacrificing a more precise quantum fluctuation treatment, and found it to be directly connected with the established Bogoliubov approach. Our predictions for the system's autocorrelation function along its direction of motion accurately reflected the expected behavior, even when fluctuations were slight. We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space that contains a specified set of Jordan curves, and investigate its properties. This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of the surfaces with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class in certain types of metric spaces. Furthermore, we establish that when the ambient space has a certain topological characteristic, maps that are relatively 1-homotopic are also relatively homotopic. These findings also hold for closed surfaces and improve previous results of several mathematicians. Additionally, we establish that within a particular relative 1-homotopy class, there is a surface with minimal area that is homeomorphic to the original surface, providing a generalization of a previous result of Monti-Saoudou-Chodise, and enabling us to solve a problem posed by G.M. Gol'dstein. Moreover, we establish that when the ambient space is topologically equivalent to the plane with a removed finite number of closed disks, the surface with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class is homeomorphic to an arc. Finally, we establish that when the ambient space is topologically equivalent to the plane with a removed closed curve, the surface with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class is either homeomorphic to that curve or it contains a neighborhood of that curve and is therefore not minimal. These findings were previously established under the assumption that the surface in question is closed. On the other hand, we provide an alternative proof of a result of Simon in the case of closed surfaces, and demonstrate that when the ambient space contains a specified set of Jordan curves that are topologically equivalent to a circle, there is a surface with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class that is homeomorphic to the original surface and contains each of those curves as a boundary component. Furthermore, we establish that when the ambient space is topologically equivalent to the plane with a removed finite number of closed curves, the surface with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class is homeomorphic to one of those curves. Finally, we solve a problem posed by G.M. Gol'dstein in the case of closed surfaces. Machine learning models often undergo performance assessment through k-fold cross-validation to facilitate model selection and parameter adjustment. Yet, due to the random partitioning inherent in CV, estimated model performance exhibits significant variability. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as demonstrated across diverse NLP tasks including sentiment analysis, part-of-speech tagging and text classification. In one such example, our research found that reducing K from 10 to 5 led to an optimal parameter set for a particular task, while also cutting down the average computation time by approximately 43%. In another instance, switching from 10-fold to 5-fold cross-validation led to a 5.6 times reduction in variance without encountering any bias, as revealed through our proposed analysis. In general, our research uncovered a negative correlation between the degree of variance and the degree of bias in j-k fold CV, as further validated through an additional 16 NLP tasks. In one such case, our research found that the optimal value of J was directly linked to the amount of training data available, suggesting that a value of $\sqrt{N}$ proved ideal, as demonstrated graphically. Initially used to achieve comparable performance with smaller student networks, these architectures have now been applied across various knowledge learning objectives such as knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. This distinct survey delves into the specifics of Teacher-Student architectures with multiple knowledge learning objectives and systematically explores knowledge construction and optimization processes, as well as analyzing various Teacher-Student architectures and learning schemes that produce robust and representative knowledge. Our FABE approach compares favourably to the current state of the art methods, particularly recursive best-first and structured message passing for the most probable explanation, as well as CPLEX, GUROBI and toulbar2 for constrained optimisation, by achieving a 5 orders of magnitude improvement in our experiments following a widely established evaluation procedure. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the influence they have on retrieving all relevant information. This research's findings have implications for various work environments that depend heavily on Web search, beyond the public sector. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. This has been demonstrated through comparative analysis with other methods, including in silico and in-experiments trials with phantom and human subjects. In experiments, scan duration was approximately 13 seconds with a field-of-view of $256mm^2$ and spatial resolution of $5.5mm^2$. This rCASPR-based method allows for continuous acquisition, continuous estimation of respiratory phases, and continuous compensation for motion, resulting in better point-spread-function, low alteration in scan duration and image contrast, and better radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. Furthermore, our method allows for the use of more stringent significance levels that Monte Carlo methods cannot achieve. We've made our code available to the public as an open-source tool. In addition to paired-permutation testing, our exact algorithm can be applied to other similar permutation tests where the test space is composed of a large number of small, non-overlapping components. We tested our method on a proxy task involving the permutation test and found it to be highly accurate. In the process of developing our method, we encountered several important questions that we couldn't answer, particularly regarding the optimal way to store and compare the structured test spaces. We hope to address these questions in future work. We believe our exact paired-permutation testing algorithm can be applied to a broad range of applications involving structured data and suggest possible areas of application such as natural language inference, where there is a need to compare the similarity between structured sentences. We've made our code available online at github.com/ExactPermutationTesting. We've also made the proxy dataset available online at github.com/StructuredPermutationEvaluation. We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space. Additionally, this triangulation's realization can be specified by a set of rules that mirror the loom's generation principles. Furthermore, the development of a veering triangulation from a loom space is shown to occur gradually, without any abrupt changes, which is a distinguishing feature. This approach also provides an alternative, more intuitive explanation for the origins of the Whitehead link's parent loom. A specific type of loom space called compact loom spaces are then examined in more detail. These spaces are found to have a veering triangulation that can be determined through a process called compactification, which involves treating the space as if it were topologically equivalent to 3D space. This leads to the discovery of a unique, embedded branch in the space, along with two subspaces: a branch domain and a branch boundary. The branch domain is then found to be topologically equivalent to the veering triangulation's 2D realization, which can be obtained from the space by removing the branch and compactifying the resulting space. This process provides a direct, and more intuitive, connection between the loom space and its associated veering triangulation. A key contribution of this research involves establishing an approach for determining the 2D realization of a veering triangulation from any loom space, which can be achieved by examining the space's branch domain. This is particularly significant because it enables the recovery of the original veering triangulation from the 2D realization of the branch domain, along with the discovery of the space's boundary in relation to the triangulation. This relationship is complex and involves the boundary's components, which can take three forms: branches that are intrinsic to the space, branches that are extrinsic to the space, and boundaries that are topologically equivalent to torus knots. This knowledge provides further insight into the intricate connection between loom spaces, veering triangulations, and the associated 2D and 3D realizations. This research on loom spaces and veering triangulations also involves examining compact loom spaces and identifying a key parameter called the space's genus, which is essential for defining and examining specific types of loom spaces called genus-n

This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted rates for the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy in the $b \bar b b \bar b \nu \bar \nu$ final state. We find that at the ILC (CLIC) with 8 ab$^{-1}$ (5 ab$^{-1}$), the discovery reach extends to magnitudes of the two leading HEFT coefficients of magnitude $\sim 0.13$ ($\sim 0.07$). High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields. The advantages of these methods, including improved numerical stability and reduced risk of FWI's trapping in local minima, are demonstrated through numerical experiments using real data. The results show that time-domain ESI yields better models than time-domain WRI, while time-domain WRI outperforms time-domain ESI in terms of computational cost. The development of WRI and ESI provides new avenues for improving seismic imaging, and the positive results obtained suggest that time-domain ESI is worthy of further exploration. The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Moreover, such a design could be adaptable to multiple TEM 
systems. Our investigation into fill-factor effects reveals possible paths to further 
reduce $d_{50}$ to as low as 0.60 Angstrom. Our study also explores the doable 
range of phase plate patterns, limiting ourselves to simple and feasible designs. 
Simplistic yet efficient designs offer promise for easy implementation across a 
variety of TEM systems. Our research was conducted using a 200 kV TEM equipped with 
an experimental programmable phase plate, and the obtained data align with previous 
reports. Our findings suggest that a phase plate with a fill-factor of 0.61 can 
attain $d_{50}$ down to 0.7 Angstrom, and that piezoelectric elements with a pixel 
density of at least 256x256 are required to efficiently control and optimize the 
electrostatic field to achieve 0.6 Angstrom resolution. Our study highlights the 
potential for a phase plate in uncorrected TEMs equipped with long-wavelength 
electrons, such as 300 kV Temmini-type TEMs. Our proposed designs also explored 
basic and advanced types, including a 3D electrostatic phase plate design that 
incorporates a level of spherical aberration correction equivalent to that of a 200 kV 
CESCOR. Our research indicates that both the resolution and current density of the 
designs are highly sensitive to the phase plate's specifications, and therefore 
temperatures, surface charges, and electrostatic fields all require precise control. 
Our study concludes by outlining the necessary specifications for future TEMs,

the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized, along with
suggested categorizations, to better understand the challenges faced. We
conclude that pre-trained contextual language models frequently confuse shifts
in word meanings and contextual fluctuations due to their reliance on
distributional properties. Moreover, they often blend the grammatical and
semantics components of words, differing from issues seen with static
embeddings. We propose multiple possible avenues for resolving these issues
in the future. For the record, we also present an initial contextualized
method from an earlier study for comparative analysis. The updated ensemble
method presented here surpasses the contextualized approach and output, with
results available in the appendix. The context-aware methods' limitations
highlight potential risks of using current contextual language models without
caution, and the findings are relevant to a range of applications including,
but not limited to, semantic change detection. The challenging cases are not
limited to words with little change; rather, they represent difficult
instances that arise in the course of everyday linguistic analysis. Such
difficult cases may even provide a window into the internal functioning of
context-aware models, offering insights that can be valuable to developers,
while also highlighting issues that contextual models face in capturing the
ambiguity of words, as well as their tendency to blend semantic and
syntactic components. The challenge of words with little change also has a
straightforward solution: it can be resolved by employing methods that
investigate the levels of change in words based on their overall historical
record, rather than through the comparison of two specific time periods.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation. Lastly, by estimating the interior structure of these asteroids, researchers found that their densities fell within a narrow range, consistent with astrophysical assumptions, which in the case of Geographos was deeper, indicating that it may have a solid core. To better understand the YORP effect and its impact on the rotation of small asteroids, future researchers are advised to conduct extensive photometric observations over long periods, which can be achieved through all-sky monitoring surveys using a network of telescopes around the world. To this end, researchers have made the light curve archive for these three asteroids freely available for further study. Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. This is accomplished by defining a distinct category of functions called locally testable (or simply tested) functions that, as expected, can be distinguished from their computable counterparts. This leads to the discovery of three distinct categories of functions: tested, computable, and undecidable functions, with tested and computable functions being mutually exclusive and each being distinct from undecidable functions. This in turn allows for the development of a two-tier structure consisting of tested and undecidable functions, with tested functions being further subdivided into continuous and non-continuous subcategories. This in turn enables the validation of a previously known but more complex result called the pumping property, as well as the discovery of a more straightforward equivalent definition for continuous functions, specifically as those that can be successfully tested against any infinite string. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. The methodologies employed can also be applied to similar research about the organization of objects and concepts. The findings of this research are relevant to various fields including anthropology, psychology, philosophy, and biology that study human conception of animals and their classification. The stimulus set used in this study consisted of 1800 high-definition color images of animals and 1800 images of other entities, with half of the images being 2D and half 3D. We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs. This modified logic, which we call QREL, enables the verification of quantum programs whose behavior is defined by equality, inclusion, or exclusion of output distributions, as well as programs that transfer classical or quantum information between pairs of programs. Furthermore, QREL facilitates the verification of programs whose behavior satisfies particular statistical properties, such as satisfying a particular Chernoff bound or having a minimum average distance between output distributions. We have also demonstrated that the verification of programs using QREL can be achieved through the application of a relevant theorem, which in turn requires the evaluation of a particular expectation that can be computed using the trace distance or the statistical distance between output distributions. We have further extended QREL to enable the verification of programs that consist of multiple program components, whose pre-/postconditions are specified as expectations over the outputs of subprograms, thereby enabling the specification and validation of complex programs that comprise multiple program components, whose behavior must satisfy a particular relationship when comparing pairs of programs. This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as $R_0$. We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. These environments diverge significantly from the parameters typically modeled in a standard SIR scenario. The simulation provides quantitative insights into these variables, which are crucial for predicting the progression of an epidemic fueled by a super-spreader event. Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with the collection L(X) of continuous linear operators that act on X. This paper seeks to expand the concept of codiskcyclicity, initially developed for a solitary operator within L(X), to a broader context of operator sets defined as $\Gamma\subset L(X).$ Some key results regarding codiskcyclic collections of operators are proven, accompanied by a codiskcyclicity criterion. Furthermore, we demonstrate its practical utility by investigating the codiskcyclicity of C_0-semigroups comprised of operators. Additionally, a specific example related to a semigroup of operators is provided. Moreover, we establish that codiskcyclicity is equivalent to the convergence of an operator's mean value for a specific operator, and also for a significant portion of a C_0-semigroup's operators. Lastly, we discuss the potential applications of these findings to the codiskcyclicity of operator systems, including those defined on the space C_0, using the notion of regular matrix theory.

Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, accounting for both local and native components. Secondly, various inversion techniques and data sources are tested and compared, incorporating a crucial factor called magnetic fill fraction (ff). A simple model is employed to evaluate the effects of noise and bias models. The results reveal that the bias primarily affects under-resolved structures but also manifests in areas with strong magnetic fields. Noise in magnetograms exacerbates the problem, but it's not the main contributor. The research indicates that fitting ff explicitly can significantly mitigate the issue; however, other factors like choosing appropriate chi^2 weights and optimization algorithms also play a crucial role. Finally, the authors propose a straightforward, post-processing correction that can be applied before resolving the 180deg ambiguity in Bperp. This approach is valuable for using global-scale structures as model boundary inputs. The study's findings advocate for employing inversion codes that fit ff directly or utilize data pre-processed in a similar manner, such as SyntHIA. A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Consequently, we are able to successfully simulate a range of models that have been inaccessible in the past, including the hubbard model at finite temperatures and half-filling, using Monte Carlo methods with a small number of complex-valued neural network parameters. Our simulations yield accurate results, with the complex-valued network's performance comparable to that of a direct rejection Monte Carlo method while significantly expanding the reach of simulations beyond what was previously possible. The proposed architecture is also applicable to other integral transformation methods plagued by an excessive determinant cost. The code for the complex-valued neural network is available at https://github.com/AyaneTerano/Complex_NN_Signet Mitigation. If σ is recognizable and letter-to-letter, then p_Y and p_X grow at similar rates, whereas if σ isn't letter-to-letter, there are instances where p_X isn't proportional to p_Y. As a result, topological entropy h_X isn't necessarily preserved when applying σ to X, indicating that defining topological entropy for free group currents F_N isn't feasible. Nevertheless, we can distinguish currents with or without zero or positive topological entropy. Additionally, we determine that for a given h, there are compact sets within the space of free group currents that are invariant to basis changes and have topological entropy less than h. Moreover, for a given h, there are currents with zero or positive topological entropy that are invariant to basis changes and have topological entropy greater than h. Finally, we find that the SolleveldelaOlivieraThiebolt curve isn't invariant to basis changes, indicating that there are basis changes that increase its topological entropy. Nonetheless, the modified curve has constant complexity for large enough n, indicating that its topological entropy is zero. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments. ReCross delivers superior performance in multiple cross-task generalization scenarios, including both within-domain and more challenging across-domain settings, without incurring additional dietary costs compared to baseline methods. The code for this project is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ASD5/Across-Task-Generalization-via-Retrieval-Augmentation.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. The code is available at: https://github.com/Haoshainie/DP-Hyperparameter-Tuning. The findings of this study are significant contributions to the field of artificial intelligence, which is currently dependent on hyperparameter tuning by the framework of machine learning models. The paper's results have implications for reducing unnecessary computations and avoiding data bottlenecks that often hinder real-world applications of machine learning. The findings of the paper provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners in the field of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and statistics, and present new research directions, such as the development of more effective and efficient methods of hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. The results of the paper also highlight the importance of carefully selecting performance and privacy loss functions for both Bayesian and evolutionary methods. The results of the paper can be improved further, and this can be achieved by conducting additional experiments using other datasets and other cost-effective algorithms of hyperparameter tuning. The results of the paper can be enhanced by incorporating suitable regularization techniques such as early stopping and dropout in the models used for performance estimation, and by conducting additional research on the development of more effective and efficient methods of hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. Additionally, we derive connections between these boolean complexes and the combinatorial properties of reduced words, as well as deterministic sequences generated by the Coxeter numbering system. Both of these results can be applied to a broader class of partially ordered sets. Lastly, we conclude by examining the boolean complex of an permutation group of degree 3, demonstrating that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection consisting of a single sphere with dimension 1 for the permutation group S_3, but differs significantly for larger permutation groups S_n for n ≥ 4.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Our study's findings have implications for designing effective strategies to control the spread of online misinformation. Our research analyzed Weibo data containing 1,485 COVID-19-related rumors collected between January 2020 and June 2020, incorporating a wide range of features that are readily available on the platform. Our model's performance was evaluated through a split experiment in which we divided the data set into training and testing subsets, applying 70% for training and 30% for validation. Our study's discoveries have important practical value in assisting platforms in identifying high-risk rumors and implementing targeted prevention measures to reduce anxiety-related propagation factors. Our research can also contribute to the development of more sophisticated algorithms for predicting the dynamics of rumor propagation and managing the spread of online misinformation. Our study's findings have been published in the IEEE Access journal. A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Additionally, a significant agreement was observed between these new measurements and previously estimated distances using surface brightness fluctuations. The accuracy of the planned $H{\rm band}$ mass estimates for the galaxies will depend on obtaining reliable measurements of their K-band magnitudes, and the potential for the forthcoming Euclid mission to significantly enhance the planetary nebulae analysis through more comprehensive observations across a broader spectral range is also discussed. The comprehensive data set of extragalactic planetary nebulae, galaxy mass distributions, and velocity dispersions presented here will continue to be valuable resources for the scientific community. The procedural methods for selecting genuine planetary nebulae sources and validating the accuracy of the planned $H{\rm band}$ mass estimates for the galaxies are also potentially applicable to ongoing and future surveys. The newly calculated distances to the galaxies will also contribute to ongoing studies of the composition and evolution of the Fornax cluster. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. With its capacity to execute sub-second analyses on massive datasets, LifeStream enables safer and more effective medical diagnoses through realistic simulations. The underlying technology in LifeStream is also applicable to other periodic stream processing applications in various domains. The source code for LifeStream is available at \url{https://github.com/aliabadi/StreamDB}.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space. Specifically, we derive its key equations and show that a curve is a timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve if and only if it can be expressed as the sum of two simple Bertrand curves with one being spacelike and the other being timelike. Furthermore, we establish that the geodesic Bertrand curves in the (1,3)-space are equivalent to the curves that satisfy a specific modification of the Frenet-Serret theorem, and whose osculating plane remains constant throughout the curve's length. This condition is met by the curves that can be described using a constant vector in their direction and whose normal component is directly proportional to the distance from a fixed point. This results in the classification of the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curves into three categories: those with a planar osculating bundle, those with a cylindrical osculating bundle with a constant radius, and those with a hyperbolic osculating bundle. This study also defines the concept of the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve in the context of a Riemannian Bertrand manifold and demonstrates that it is equivalent to the curves whose natural equation is given by a specific differential-recursive method. This results in the classification of the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curves in a Riemannian Bertrand manifold of any dimension as the curves whose natural vector field satisfies the differential-recursive equation derived from its intrinsic properties. This generalised version of the timelie (1,3)-Bertrand curve can be applied to any dimensional space and provides an innovative approach to studying the curves in a Riemannian Bertrand manifold. This research also provides an innovative solution to the problem of defining the concept of the Bertrand curve in the context of a manifold. The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To demonstrate this, we employ a straightforward yet effective approach that involves simultaneously optimizing the network parameters and the loss function using a simple meta-learning strategy. Our experiments on numerous datasets showcase the benefits of this approach, which can be interpreted as a form of transfer learning. Our findings are further validated by examining the connection between the proposed approach and traditional transfer learning. Our research highlights the potential of adaptive loss functions in enhancing model performance and facilitating seamless domain adaptation, which can be particularly valuable guidelines for the deep learning community. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ghru/AdaptiveLoss.

Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A key finding here is that the response of the superconducting order parameter to the applied magnetic field can result in the enlargement of the coexistence region of the superconducting and metallic phases in doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification. In particular, the proposed approach is applied to three well-known CPM formats: MSK, GMSK, and MINSEK, yielding preferred delay periods for each. In general, the proposed method is valuable for any conventional differential detection system, whereas specifically for CPM systems, the proposed approach may be further improved by exploring other optimization criteria. In addition, the research emphasizes the significance of testing schemes, including both ideal and real-world channels, and presents numerical outcomes for ease of reference. In response to performance degradation caused by excessive delay periods, the paper introduces an alternative detection technique with superior signal-to-noise ratio with minimal performance degradation, primarily beneficial for systems experiencing slow channel variations. In such scenarios, the proposed approach results in nearly coherent detection performance, as demonstrated by the MINSEK example. In this context, Coherent Differential Detection (CDD) is presented as a less complicated alternative to coherent detection methods. The proposed approach may also be applied to other modulation systems similar to CPM. In particular, for systems with low delay periods, the proposed method allows for seamless transition to coherent detection systems with minimal modification required, as shown by the MSK example. This is accomplished by determining the thermodynamic quantities known as heat capacity and quantum compressibility in model spacetimes filled with a quantum field at both high and low temperatures. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  Our exploration into both isolated and controlled settings uncovers a wide range of applications for these models including conversational interactions, text generation, and description of image content.  Our open-source toolkit, available for public use, enables researchers to experiment with different formulations of conditional relationships and provides a platform for developing tools that can automatically generate these relationships from raw data.  Our analysis into both individual rules and massive subsets of these relationships has implications for our understanding of intentional actions, intentional goals, and the elements that make up our daily experience.  Ultimately, our findings validate the utility of datasets describing contextual relationships as a means of guiding the development of artificial intelligence.  Our work on ATOMIC has been utilized in a range of subsequent experiments including a system of structured conversations, a framework for generating multi-sentence descriptions of images, a system for answering questions centered on everyday experience, and a model of low-frequency text generation.  Our proposed dataset and tools for interacting with it are available at https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1C9gJlhB9z-68A5OdB5EJL0Tg-6HhL9D5.

Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization and reutilization, and Quantum Conditional Logic. Moreover, NISQ-HHL integrates an enhanced Phase Estimation executed on actual hardware, namely the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1, alongside a novel approach to determine the optimal duration of Hamiltonian simulation. This research centers on portfolio optimization but presents solutions applicable to any problem addressed via HHL within the Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum era. The associated code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Qiskit-Advantage/Portfolio-Optimization. The research was conducted using the Qiskit Advantage Simulator and the Quantinuum System Model H1-1. The findings were compared to a naive classical implementation and a pre-existing quantum solution, revealing the potential for hybrid quantum-classical portfolio optimization on NISQ hardware. The optimal duration $\Delta t$ of Hamiltonian simulation was found to be directly proportional to the square of the number of eigenvalue discrepancies between the target matrix and the surrogate matrix, and the results suggest that in the Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum era, the Procrustes method may yield comparable outcomes to the Lagrange multiplier method. The research highlights the challenges posed by qubit reinitialization and reutilization, and the findings suggest that the threshold for harmonic mean connectivity should be set relatively low. The research also explores the issue of quantum noise-induced bias and proposes a novel solution, alongside the introduction of a hybrid version of the Monte Carlo Phase Estimation method. The findings are validated across multiple realistic scenarios, including scenarios with varying levels of noise, different quantization levels, and with and without reinitialization, reutilization, and noise-induced bias. To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied. Moreover, the model's robustness to noisy conditions is demonstrated by a 12.37% reduction in word error rate on the NASA SENTINEL-2 dataset. The code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghru/BidirectionalMultiModal.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. The paper also discusses an alternative proof of the asymptotic uniformity of the first $k_n$ parking locations, which is based on a different argument that involves bounded functions of the walk and the use of the large deviation principle. The consequences of these distances and the conditioned random walk formulation are explored and presented in the paper. The results obtained in this study can be viewed as specific cases of a more broad statement that we also derive, which enables us to directly apply our proofs to a more general scenario. The general statement, which is formulated in Theorem 2, can be thought of as a statement about the asymptotic behavior of functions of a Markov chain and may have value to itself. The paper also discusses the connection between the two distance metrics used and presents an example that illustrates the difference between them. Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings. The occurrence of periodic variations and period shifts could be indicative of a more complex scenario, potentially related to the unique properties of the nanowires or their interaction with the gate electrode. The measurement of self-flux expulsion in nanowires at zero applied magnetic field also supports this viewpoint. The period shifts during measurements could be related to the occurrence of phase slips or another unknown mechanism but do not align with explanations based on Coulomb blockade or the granular nature of the nanowires. The interaction between the nanowires and the gate electrode offers a means of investigating the occurrence of self-sustained oscillations in the conductance of the nanowires, potentially shedding light on the underlying physics. The possibility of examining the relationship between the nanowires' interface and the magnetic properties of the material by manipulating the gate electrode and thus the superconducting state of the nanowires also arises. The discovery of a hysteretic response in the conductance of the nanowires at zero applied magnetic field also presents new questions about the magnetic properties of the NbN material used. Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views. Our code is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghulamai/novel-view-prediction.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses. In considering the practical applications of our findings, we propose several modifications to the 'well mixed' model that would make it more effective for predicting the dissemination of diseases in similar environments. In analyzing the spread of a hypothetical respiratory disease within an urban bus, our results showed that the modified 'well mixed' model accurately captured the dynamics of the situation, with the differences in outcomes being minimal when comparing it to the detailed model used. The study demonstrated that with appropriate ventilation strategies, a 'well mixed' model can also provide valuable insights for reducing the risk of transmission within these confined spaces. In summarizing our findings, we emphasize that while a 'well mixed' model is useful for predicting the dissemination of diseases, it should be used in conjunction with the available knowledge on airflow dynamics. In addition, several open research questions were identified in this study, with solutions being essential for further improving our understanding of the dynamics of airflow and aerosol transport in complex environments. In considering these challenges, we believe that collaboration between experts from various fields will be necessary, with the outcome being a better 'well mixed' model that can provide a more accurate prediction of disease transmission in urban buses and similar enclosed settings. In analyzing the spread of a simulated SARS outbreak within an urban bus, our results showed that the difference in the recovery rates rather than the ventilation rates had a more significant impact on the distribution of the virus. In contrast, the spread of the disease was significantly influenced by the ventilation rates when analyzing the situation with a 50% recovery rate. In further examining this phenomenon, we found that a more rapid recovery rate will result in a higher concentration of the virus in the air, with the outcome being a greater discrepancy in the distribution of the virus. In considering this finding, we believe that it will be relevant to a broader range of situations beyond urban buses

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets. The development of an intuitive understanding of how enforcing Lipschitz continuity reduces overfitting is also presented. This understanding is reflected in the results obtained when applying the approach to challenging classification tasks. We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies. This work is part of a broader effort to simulate other processes involving vector leptoquarks, such as those involving a single electron or muon, which are crucial for uncovering evidence of these exotic particles, if they exist. This code is an open contribution to the community, available through a public repository, and we outline its structure and potential customizations for users. This code can simulate a range of processes, including those involving a single lepton and ditau pairs, at the level of precision required for ongoing and future searches at the LHC. This work can also be used to develop similar simulations for other processes, which could provide insights into the properties of vector leptoquarks, given the constraints of their possible existence based on current data. Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings. The code is available at https://github.com/ghd143/PMNet.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems are not necessarily improved by considering the ideas underlying CT. Furthermore, the study finds that these computer systems already incorporate the coherence information required to recognize connections within the text, making CT's contribution limited. Additionally, the study discusses aspects that influence connections within the text but are not accounted for by CT, including the systems' knowledge and their tendency to favor more recent statements. By incorporating these elements, the study presents a revised version of CT and shows that it better captures the connections within the text compared to the original CT. The revised version of CT also provides insights into the structure of the text and can be used to generate more coherent sequences of statements. The study's findings are supported by multiple examples and graphs that illustrate the revised version of CT in action. The development of the revised version of CT is made possible by the use of a free computer-available summary of centering theory, which is also presented in the study. The study's results have important implications for creating computer systems that generate coherent sequences of statements, including the use of reverse order of the text as a simple and effective method to increase coherence. The study's findings related to the relationships within the text can be verified by any researcher using the available data and computer system. The study's results related to the generation of coherent sequences of statements are demonstrated through a working demonstration available online. The development of the revised version of CT and the resulting insights are also applicable to other tasks that involve understanding the coherence of the text, including but not limited to identifying connections within the text. The study's results provide a way to quantify the coherence of the text and can be used as a metric to evaluate the coherence of the text in tasks that involve understanding the coherence of the text. The study's results related to the use of reverse order of the text as a simple and effective method to increase coherence also have important implications for creating computer systems that generate coherent sequences of statements, including but not limited to the current computer system. The study's results can be verified by any researcher using the available data and computer system

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among different machine learning algorithms utilizing a wide range of evaluation metrics, including their scalability to accommodate diverse real-world datasets. The results showed that the CBR (Case-Based Reasoning) algorithm yielded the most accurate and reliable outcomes on previously unseen datasets, exceeding the performance of alternative methods by 25% according to the ranking of overall performance evaluation. To validate these findings, an independent dataset from a real-world application was utilized. The novel approach developed was then integrated into the CBR model, and the resulting hybrid system outperformed the existing state-of-the-art methods and algorithms evaluated in this research. The novel approach developed also yielded results that closely matched the ground truth on an additional independent dataset, further demonstrating its versatility and capability to handle diverse real-world datasets with minimal modification. The findings of this research have significant implications for various real-world applications and scenarios involving WiFi-based distance estimation, including but not limited to WiFi-based location estimation, indoor mapping, WiFi-based crowd management, and search and rescue operations in disaster scenarios. The novel approach developed provides a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments with diverse real-world datasets and has been made available online for download by interested researchers and practitioners. The results of this research have also highlighted the significance of selecting appropriate feature extraction and machine learning algorithms crucial for enhancing the accuracy of WiFi-based distance estimation. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. Furthermore, the research highlights a more significant impact of beam breakup instability called the average beam breakup point, which can influence design parameters like the number of passes, average charge, and charge multiplication schemes. Combining this with studies on recirculation schemes and beam breakup instability, this paper presents a comprehensive analysis of average beam breakup point, charge distribution, and filling patterns to explore previously unoptimized energy recovery linac designs. Such analysis facilitates easier implementation of beam breakup instability effects into design optimization problems using multi-objective and multi-parameter models. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation, the US Department of Energy, and the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The associated code is available for public use.
