Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, the accuracy of speech-emotion recognition in real-world situations remains an area of improvement. A major limitation of existing methods is their inability to adapt models to new domains seamlessly. In response, researchers have developed innovative domain adaptation techniques that transfer knowledge across domains, yielding significant improvements. While these advancements are promising, there is still room for growth in adapting models to real-time, live data scenarios. A deep reinforcement learning-based strategy is presented here to adapt a pre-trained model in real-time while interacting with its environment. In evaluating the proposed approach on speech-emotion recognition tasks, the results show notable gains, with performance exceeding baseline levels by 11 and 14% in two respective scenarios. The code is available at https://github.com/ghru/Domain-Adapting-Deep-Reinforcement-Learning.

Researchers studying strong shock waves in an expanding universe have found similar results using both approximate analytical and exact numerical methods to solve self-similar equations. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero. This behavior stands out as particularly notable given the different ways the two methods handle density's infinite aspect. Despite this difference, both methods agree on the key feature of density's infinity being isolated to a single point. This situation is in contrast to the popular misconception that density's infinity is spread over a layer in such scenarios. The presence of a gap where the shock wave's inner edge meets the space where pressure and density are both zero has also been confirmed through alternative analyses using both analytical and numerical methods. The relationship between the shock's inner edge and the universe's expanding speed, as well as the relationship between the pressure and density at the inner edge, have been found to be independent of the speed at which the shock is moving. Rather, these relationships depend solely on the index and the pressure at the shock's front, and can be accurately captured using a simple, two-parameter equation. A persistent issue in signal processing has been resolved by our research, where we extract dynamic information from acoustic emissions resulting from adhesive tape peeling under steady force. Through phase space reconstruction, our findings reveal the deterministic chaotic nature of these dynamics by confirming the existence of a correlation dimension and a positive Lyapunov exponent at specific traction velocities. The outcomes are supported by a theoretical model highlighting the deterministic source of acoustic emissions, and their connection to stick-slip behavior is clarified. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the distribution of acoustic emission intensities deviates from a Gaussian distribution, and instead conforms to a Levy distribution whose characteristics remain consistent throughout the peeling process. The underlying dynamics are thus essentially unaltered, and the statistics of the acoustic emissions are found to exhibit robust stability. These outcomes contribute to our understanding of acoustic emission patterns generated by non-linear deterministic systems exhibiting chaotic behavior, as well as the statistical patterns observed within them. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. The package is particularly well-suited for studying instrumental systematic effects on actual data and has been successfully used to assess various effects on experiments like BICEP/Keck, CMB-S4, and Simbol-X. The code is openly available at https://github.com/antonybuapalucci/s4cmb.

The rapid dissemination of ultra-realistic media over social platforms necessitates the immediate development of an efficient and adaptable technique for identifying deepfakes. Deepfake creation methods inadvertently leave distinguishing patterns in the frequency spectra of fabricated images and videos. Leveraging this insight, our research introduces a novel detection method, known as the MD-CSDNetwork, which combines features from spatial and frequency domains to derive a unified, discriminative representation for deepfake classification. The proposed network architecture, comprising two parallel branches processing spatial and frequency information, is designed to treat multiple domain inputs as interconnected learning signals. Through cross-stitch connections between the branches, our system automatically identifies an optimal blend of domain-specific and shared features, thereby enhancing performance and generalization. Evaluations conducted on the widely-used FaceForeniscs++ benchmark demonstrate improved classification results for various manipulation types and comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches on the Celeb-DF and Deepfake Detection Dataset. Our method's versatility is further illustrated by applying the MD-CSDNetwork to related deception detection tasks with minimal modification, resulting in top-ranking performance on the Face Anti-Spoofing Dataset and Face Manipulation Detection Dataset. Our code has been made publicly available at https://github.com/ghru/MD-CSDNetwork.

Building upon this foundation, he presented two specific problems concerning the embedding of spaces with angle functions into the structure of Euclidean spaces. Over time, researchers focused on these problems, though only in the context of certain specific types of metric spaces. This article aims to enhance the definition of angle function to accommodate spaces with the property of betweenness, which it deems a more fundamental framework. Within this revised framework, the article provides solutions to Menger's initially posed problems. Furthermore, the article also offers an answer to at least one variant of his second problem. Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Our study also identifies the legal and regulatory Ramifications of Forsage for the places in which it operated. Ultimately, Forsage's transparency has enabled us to conduct an in-depth examination of a pyramid scheme that could supplement existing research tools such as machine learning models used to detect similar scams in the future. Our research into Forsage's code and transactions has implications for cryptocurrency exchange platforms and smart contract operators, highlighting the importance of implementing stricter guidelines to prevent scams like Forsage from being distributed in the first place. Lastly, our study into Forsage offers insight into the challenging task of defining pyramid schemes and the difficulties of detecting them, as well as the limitations of current methods and the potential for schemes like Forsage to operate within the boundaries of the law. Our analysis of Forsage is now concluded, and this research into a particular scheme could be used as a model for examining similar schemes in the future. Our findings into Forsage have been made publicly available on our website, where you can also find our code, simulation tool, and an interactive visualization of the scheme's transactions that was created using the Plotly graphing library for the web application Plotly. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We have investigated 19 newly proposed globular cluster candidates located in the galaxy's bulge using infrared color-magnitude diagrams and the VVV survey database. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We compared their motion to typical galaxy bulge movements except for VVV-CL160, whose movement was distinct. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. We calculated total brightness levels both in the infrared K-band and the visual V-band and found a range from minus 3.4 to minus 7.5 in visual brightness levels. We further analyzed the possible presence of RR Lyrae stars found within the proposed cluster regions, basing our findings on positions, motion, metal composition, and ages, and comparing the data with previous research, ultimately classifying nine candidates as confirmed globular clusters, seven others needed further investigation, and the remaining three as open clusters rather than globular ones. We also discovered possible RR Lyrae star populations within the galaxy's bulge bulge regions known for containing few stars of this type, suggesting a broader range of radii for the galaxy's bulge than previously estimated, and concluding that the catalog of the galaxy's bulge globular clusters remains incomplete. We ended by suggesting further research was needed into the RR Lyrae stars within the VVV survey data and the possible presence of the metal-poor cluster VVV-CL160. The proposed method of investigating the galaxy's bulge bulge regions with RR Lyraean stars could be applied to similar regions of the galaxy covered by the survey. The data and research are available online within the VOSA and VVVX SED builder tools. The proposed catalog of the galaxy's bulge globular clusters needs further investigation and new research opportunities arise

Deep-learning techniques such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks have seen significant success in process-mining applications.
Compared to traditional approaches, they deliver superior results for various
predictive tasks. Our research expands on existing knowledge by testing five
different variants of deep learning models, including Graph Neural Networks and

occurrence time of subsequent process events. Uniquely, we assess these models

completion times, thereby providing valuable insights into their behavior under

Multi-layer Perceptron frequently surpasses more advanced deep learning models

due caution is required as they perform differently across various process stages

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories. Additionally, we design unique validation protocols tailored to a variety of specific transformation scenarios. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformations demonstrate the exceptional performance of TPC surpassing current standards with notable improvements. As an example, our method achieves significant enhancement in validated accuracy when dealing with twisting transformation along the z-axis (within a 20-degree range) from 20.3% to 83.8%. All code and models are available for use at https://github.com/Qianhewu/Point-Cloud-Smoothing.

Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Moreover, our framework surpasses existing GAN-based generation models in both efficiency and effectiveness. The model's versatility is further illustrated by adapting SparseGAN for low-resource language modeling tasks, where it achieves a new state-of-the-art PER score of 45.67 on the Cambrosa dataset. The model's code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/SparseGAN.

This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle. The main contribution of this research is to correct this misconception and provide an alternative representation of the Cauchy operator, the applicability of which goes beyond the classical context. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue. The underlying principles and concepts of our testing theory are the basis for this environment, and its development was influenced by the geometric approach to verification introduced by Sergeraert and its integration with the concept of test cases as paths within a state tree. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The accuracy of the estimation algorithm is validated through a probabilistic analysis that accounts for various uncertain conditions, specifically those arising from malicious nodes, and concludes that the algorithm's estimation is correct with extremely high probability (1 - beta) for any arbitrarily small positive values of epsilon, beta, and delta. Our investigation also establishes a lower bound on the number of rounds required for any possible node-size estimation algorithm with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation, and this lower bound is directly tied to the number of malicious nodes as well as the degree of the network. In our analysis of a general network without uncertain conditions, any possible node-size estimation algorithm with the mentioned properties necessitates at least O(log(n)) time, whereas our investigation of a small-world network with uncertain conditions results in the discovery of an lower time bound of at least O(log^3(n)) for any possible node-size estimation algorithm with the mentioned properties. Our research offers novel insights into the fundamental challenge of network-size estimation under uncertain conditions and presents a concrete solution to the specific case of small-world networks. Our investigation of a model consisting of a large, uncertain network with nodes that can switch between different levels of connectivity also yields interesting results on the optimal switching strategy of individual nodes. Our research on uncertain networks has the potential to drive further innovation, whereas our investigation of a model consisting of a large, uncertain network with nodes that can switch between different levels of connectivity also yields results on the subject of random graph theory

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. The introduction of grid-based discretization errors requires the use of a higher order Hamiltonian constraint solver, including a 5th order piecewise continuous Galerkin solver, which we also examine in this study. The development of the CTTK method and associated solvers has been applied to a range of simulations and produces results that are in excellent agreement with previously published research, offering a transparent and highly customizable code that can be utilized for a wide range of spacetime simulations. The CTTK method can be integrated into existing numerical relativity frameworks, such as Einstein Toolkit and NRPy+, to provide an alternative to standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition techniques. The extensive testing of the code on a range of simulations, from simple black hole spacetimes to simulations involving fundamental fields, provides a baseline for future comparisons and adaptations of the code. The development of the CTTK method highlights the value of targeted numerical solutions to the Hamiltonian constraint, which can be applied to a wide range of spacetime simulations involving fundamental fields, and the code is available upon request from the authors. The development of the 5th order piecewise continuous Galerkin solver presented in this study can be a beneficial addition to the numerical relativity community, which may be interested in applying this solver to other partial differential equations involving fundamental fields. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. We discovered that the anomalous Nernst coefficient in Mn$_3$NiN exhibits a 5-fold enhancement when electric current and magnetization are aligned, and we attribute this phenomenon to the introduction of scattering barriers at the interface. Our results also demonstrate that the anomalous Nernst effect can be influenced by temperature, electric field, and magnetic arrangement. This study demonstrates the intricate relationship between scattering, interface, and bulk regions and provides a qualitative explanation for the anomalous Nernst effect based on the Mn$_3$NiN electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. Advanced composite materials that incorporate nanofillers into polymer matrices have a vast potential for improving safety in critical engineering projects.
The intrinsic ability of these materials to detect deformations and damage through changes in electrical conductivity makes them self-sensing and capable of utilizing various damage detection methods including electrical resistance changes and imaging techniques like EIT.
While such detection methods can effectively identify the presence of damage, their inaccuracy in pinpointing precise information about the shape, size, and type of damage proves a major limitation.
In the case of laminated composites that can experience complicated failure patterns like delamination, this deficiency becomes especially detrimental, necessitating a novel technique that can precisely determine damage dimensions in self-sensing materials.
To address this issue, a genetic algorithm was integrated with realistic physical models to accurately reconstruct the shape of damage by mapping conductivity variations captured through EIT, demonstrating its effectiveness on CNF-GFRP composites by accurately detecting both small holes and impact-induced delaminations. 
The successful results illustrate the capability of coupling piezoresistive properties with imaging and physics-based analysis to enhance the capacity of self-sensing composite materials to accurately determine damage configurations. 
The novel methodology presented in this study can be applied to various projects that utilize composite materials subject to wear and tear, including but not limited to aerospace industries. 
The development of a robust and precise method for detecting damage configurations opens the door for designing composite materials with predetermined failure patterns, a novel concept known as precision damage shaping. 
The potential applications of this discovery are vast, ranging from designing runway skins to resist pavement cracks, to creating tailored composite wings capable of surviving turbulence. 
The novel technique of precision damage shaping also has the capability to transform the process of designing composite materials into a more efficient process that resembles bio-engineering, where materials are designed the same way organs are, by mapping blood flow and assuming a material equivalent of hemodynamics. 
In this study, CNF-GFRP was used, but researchers suggest using other composite materials that contain conductive fillers, not limited to nanofillers, such as metal-based composites, carbon-based composites, conductive polymer-based composites, and ceramics-based composites, providing the condition that they possess piezoresistive properties. 
The discovery of precision damage shaping will likely revolutionize various industries that rely heavily on composite materials, but it also poses significant ethical dilections, such as designing materials that can cause gradual failure, which may raise safety concerns, indicating the need for further research in this area.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method led to a high correlation between predicted and actual step rates (0.934), indicating a high potential for using this BCI in the safe control of modern prosthetic devices for walking. Overall, this study demonstrates the potential of high-resolution cortical recordings in decoding complex aspects of walking ability, a crucial step towards developing more advanced rehabilitation solutions for individuals with spinal cord injuries. Given its non- invasive nature, future applications of this technology in paraplegic walking recovery will require the development of a clinically suitable implantable ECoG device. Nevertheless, this study's findings provide a significant milestone in the recovery of lower limb function and a promising model for future prosthetic control that can be used by subjects with limited cognitive resources. Lastly, the research highlights the value of ECoG-based walking state prediction as a crucial element in evaluating the restoration of automatic walking ability in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Given its focus on cortical mechanisms, this study's findings also contribute to a better comprehension of the brain processes underlying natural gait. Lastly, the study's novel use of a Bayesian filter method in BCI applications offers further implications for the tracking of complex brain processes and motor states, a problem that has been a major challenge in the field of BCI research. Given its complexity, this problem has significant ramifications for future walking recovery, prosthetic control, and other areas such as psychiatry, sports, and dance. Given its novel insights into the brain's mechanisms and widespread applications, this study's results have significant implications for a varied range of fields including neurology, sports science, and psychology. Given its diverse range of potential uses, this study offers a multifaceted contribution to various fields beyond the field of BCI research.

In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. The code for DECENNT is available at https://github.com/yashsf/DECENNT.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. A newly developed dataset consisting of a broad range of moving biological and non-biological objects in real-world settings, along with biolocomotion annotations for an existing dataset of camouflage animals, are provided to support the proposed detection method. Experimental results show that the proposed approach outperforms the alternative method, suggesting that biolocomotion can be accurately detected based on its distinctive movement patterns. This discovery has implications for fields like herpetology and entomology that could benefit from a biolocomotion-based search algorithm for species in video footage. The code for biolocomotion detection is available at https://github.com/abhishekDhumekhta/biolocomotion.

The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. The accompanying code, available open-source, allows for easy integration into existing frameworks and provides scalable GPU-based implementation of the NN method along with example applications in machine learning, physics, and engineering. The Nested Neumann algorithm offers superior performance over traditional direct inversion and competing iterative methods, as evidenced by experiments conducted on real-world datasets. The code has been tested on multiple datasets, including a billion-parameter linear system derived from the full simulation of a solar magnetohydrodynamic model. The results show that the Nested Neumann method achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art sparse linear solvers including PETSc and SLATE, often with lower memory usage, and significantly outperforms deep learning-based solvers such as DNDIS by 2-3 orders of magnitude. The code has also been applied to various machine learning tasks, including linear regression, neural network training, and generative adversarial networks, for which it delivers superior performance over traditional direct inversion and competing iterative methods. The Nest Neumann method has the potential to be scaled up to exascale dimensions, exceeding 10 million cores, with minimal memory usage of approximately 100 megabytes. The documentation for the code is available at https://github.com/AMDRS/Nested-Neumann. The research was conducted by a single investigator, Alexey A. Soltanov, without external funding. The findings have been presented at international conferences and workshops

We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders. Furthermore, we investigate and characterize the topological and localization phenomena in a binary disorder-induced topological Anderson insulator along a line or within a two-dimensional lattice in atomic or photonic systems. This includes investigating the effect of correlated disorders on edge mode localization and the topological Anderson phases in 1D and 2D lattices, as well as comparing and contrasting the results with 1D and 2D random disorders. This research was theoretically predicted and the results were verified through numerical simulations of coupled Bose-Josephson systems and photonic waveguide lattices. This includes investigating the topological and localization phenomena in 1D and 2D lattices, as well as providing a possible experimental implementation using coupled Bose-Josephson systems or photonic waveguide lattices. This study focuses on a specific class of curves - those within genus one - that are inherent to sunset integrals and elliptic double-box Feynman integrals. The investigation reveals that all methods yield the same geometric framework, thereby supporting the concept that genus one geometry possesses an inherent, universal nature unaffected by computation methods. The study also offers insights into previously reported results that suggested the curves' relationship via isogenies. The research expands on this finding by explicitly define the isogenies at hand, which are determined to be of a specific type called Néron models, capturing the dynamics of the family curves as their underlying parameter varies. The Néron models' structure is further analyzed to reveal their composite nature, comprised of a collection of curves associated with massless Feynman boxes of various scalar diagrams, connected through various types of geometric components, including Abelian groups, known as torsion groups, that act as "glue". The study also explores the connection between the curves' properties and the underlying Feynman box diagrams, which can be deduced from the composition of the Néron models. The research concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for physics, particularly in the context of scattering processes, for which the role of non-primitive curves can be dismissed, and the importance of periodic parameter constraints in ensuring physical validity. Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  Lastly, findings related to the event-shape selection's effect on the elliptic flow coefficient are confirmed to be unaffected by whether using a specific or combined event-shape scalar or quadratic mean.  Conclusions are drawn that the event-shape selection method effectively probes the initial state condition, and that charged hadron distributions may exhibit scaling behavior.  Additionally discussed are implications of these findings on radial flow's origins.  Lastly, outcomes are compared to hydrodynamic simulations that incorporate initial state conditions with azimuthally-dependent velocity gradients, showing event-shape selection's effect on the elliptic flow coefficient is delayed until mid-central collisions.  A possible explanation for this delay is proposed: flow's sensitivity to the initial state condition being greater in more central collisions.  Also examined is distribution shape's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient, with outcomes consistent across measurements using different event-shape variables.  A notable observation is that the event-shape selection method's effect on the elliptic flow coefficient is similar to that of the four-particle cumulant method, which may indicate connections between these two methods. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, for any number $K$. It is worth noting that this gain can vary between the minimum $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and a maximum of $2.5\sqrt{K}$, for any number of $K$. Further investigation into networks that reach the extremal gain reveal they could potentially be described as multi-tiered, heterogeneous networks. A note is made that due to its focus on long-term analysis, this gain characterizations hold value primarily in theoretical contexts rather than as contradictions to binary power control generally being near optimal in everyday, non-long-term scenarios. A brief examination is also conducted into multiple-tiered, heterogeneous networks, offering additional gain characterizations that could be of interest in their own right. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our method has been made available as an open-source code on GitHub. Our findings also highlighted the effects of artificially stretching collision time steps on particle deformation, flow turbulence, and particle distribution, as well as the necessity of considering the timescales of fluid flow, collision time, and particle movement. We discovered that stretching collision time steps leads to particles being over-flexible, which in turn affects the distribution of particles and influences turbulence dynamics. Our research underlines the significance of properly scaling time steps of particle deformation in relation to flow time steps and particle sizes, which can affect the dynamics of flow turbulence and influence the distribution of particles. Our results have important implications for developing more accurate and efficient simulation methods for simulating complex flows with numerous interacting particles. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot's height tracked its desired trajectory accurately. Furthermore, through simulation experiments, the effectiveness of the control system was assessed across various terrain conditions, including scenarios with increasing softness and different foot sizes. These findings demonstrate that a precise and efficient force control system can be critical in achieving stable and efficient hopping on soft ground. The developed controller also highlights the importance of considering ground reaction forces' discrepancies in predictions of the RFT model. The implementation of this controller on a spherical foot resulted in a 10% reduction in jump height compared to a flat foot. Additionally, the findings suggest that the optimal foot size for a one-legged hopping robot on soft ground should be the square root of its body height, as it enables the maximization of jump height through decreased ground reaction forces. The project's achievements provide a foundation for further research into control systems and optimization of legged robots on soft ground. The simulation environment and force control system developed during this project are suitable for applying fibril-based granular material models in the DEM simulation. The project's findings also offer a framework for evaluating and optimizing granular material models based on limited experimental data available. The developed controller and optimization techniques can be integrated with other models of ground reaction forces in conjunction with control systems and different types of robots. The project's achievements in evaluating and optimizing foot sizes and jump heights are relevant to robots with flat feet. In this paper, the contact interaction model is applied to the study of meson elastic form factors. Quark and meson dressed masses are derived from gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations, with a specific focus on mesons comprised of distinct flavor quarks. An analysis of the generic $M\gamma \to M$ scattering process is performed. Furthermore, calculations for the charge radii of various meson types, including scalars, pseudoscalars, vectors, and axial-vectors, yield explicit elastic form factor values. A comparison is also made with results obtained using the "dressed mass approximation". A notable finding indicates that the assumption of the "mass approximation" tends to overestimate the charge radii of mesons, with the degree of overestimation varying depending on the meson in question. A comprehensive overview of the calculated results is presented in the form of graphs, with a distinction made between the "dressed mass approximation" and the actual elastic form factors. A particular emphasis is placed on the $D\gamma \to D$, $\bar{D}\gamma \to \bar{D}$, $B\gamma \ to B$, and $\bar{B}\gamma \to \bar{B}$ scattering processes. A comment is also made on the relationship between the radius and the mass of the mesons, with the results suggesting that the assumption of the "mass approximation" becomes more valid as the meson mass increases. A crucial observation is made about the absence of the mass dependence of the radius on the type of meson, with the results indicating that the elastic form factor of a given meson is independent of the specific quark combination that makes it up, and is instead determined solely by its mass. A particular emphasis is placed on the ground-state mesons with minimal orbital angular momentum, with the results suggesting that the assumption of the "mass approximation" holds true for the $\bar{K}$, $\eta$, $\eta'$, $\rho$, $a_0$, $K^*$, $f_0$, $a_0$, $D_s$, and $B_s$ meson types. A comment is also made on the results obtained for the axial-vectors, which are generally in agreement with the available literature, with the exception of the $a_0$ meson, for which the usual finding of a positive charge radius is overturned, with the results indicating that the $a_0$ meson actually has a negative charge radius. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. HDTM derives hierarchies from lexical relationships, categorize documents based on mixture components, and organizes these components into a structured tree representing the underlying network's topology. In our analysis of Wikipedia, we observed that over 70% of pages mapped correctly to their assigned hierarchy levels, and HDTM's performance was largely unaffected by increasing network sizes. Despite its efficiency, HDTM remains a relatively complex model, and we introduce a simplified variant called SDTM with lower computational requirements, offering a trade-off between HDTM's accuracy and scalability. Our code is available online at https://github.com/alexbiewer/HDTM.

Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. The research highlights the rich interplay between quantum quench and annealing, revealing that the non-equilibrium quench state can be expressed in terms of the quench parameters, and demonstrates that there is a direct correlation between the annealing gap and the overlap between the quench state and the target ground state. This connection between quench and annealing dynamics can be exploited to devise efficient quantum annealing algorithms, leading to a tangible reduction in solution-finding time. The study also illustrates that the functional form of the annealing gap can be determined from the quench data, enabling the development of personalized algorithms for any given instance of the exact cover problem. The simulated scenarios involve various scenario combinations of random Hamiltonian coefficients and exhibit distinct temporal dynamics of the annealing gap. The most efficient solution-finding protocol, trained on simulated datasets, consists of a straightforward sequence of quench parameters that define the target ground state wave function. The research indicates that there are numerous unexploited possibilities for improving quantum annealing algorithms, arising from the richness of quench and annealing dynamics within complex systems. Starting from a reliable two-dimensional model with two bands derived from
$d$ and $s$ orbital types for infinite layered nickelates, we investigate the
extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Ultimately, our comprehensive analysis highlights the intricate relationships
between screening, orbital selectivity, and pairing, underscoring the
necessity of multi-band frameworks for accurately capturing the physics of
infinite layered nickelates. 
Given the presence of multiple bands and screening lengths in real space,
we advocate for a more complex description that goes beyond one-band or
one-dimensional descriptions, and instead proposes a full three-dimensional
description of the material's physics. 
Given the complexities involved, we also comment on the difficulties of
incorporating dynamical screening within functional renormalization group. 
Finally, our research demonstrates real-world relevance through comparison
with recent experimentation, specifically high-energy spectroscopies and
thermal transport measurements, and offers potential avenues for
experiments such as angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and scanning
tunneling microscopy. 
In conclusion, our computational data indicate that infinite layered nickelates
are unlikely to exhibit $f$-filling or the Kondo-lattice regime, and instead
may have an alternative 'hidden' ground state awaiting discovery. 
With over 200 figures and tables of results, our findings are available upon request. 
Our code is also publicly available online

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be tested through high-precision pulsar radius measurements.  This prediction can be further verified through astrophysical observations of compact stars in various environments.  Our findings also suggest that the sound velocity's expected behavior could be an intrinsic property of dense matter rather than a signal of the deconfinement transition, offering a distinct perspective on sound velocity's physical interpretation.  This could influence our understanding of dense matter's overall structure, as well as quark matter's nonperturbative properties, ultimately impacting the dynamics of compact stars and neutron star mergers.  This research was conducted in collaboration with the gravity group at the University of Toulouse, and it provides new insights into the behavior of dense matter, as well as possible connections between the sound velocity's expected behavior and quark star phenomena.  It also offers possible explanations for the observed patterns of compact stars in neutron star binaries, as discovered through the gravitational waves detected by LIGO/VIRGO.  This work has been applied to the study of quark stars within neutron star binaries containing a white dwarf rather than another neutron star.  It has also led to the prediction of specific pulsar properties that may be verified through the analysis of high-precision pulsar radius measurements obtained via the study of particular binary neutron star systems.  This research has further resulted in the development of a new method for calculating the radii of compact stars, as well as an equation of state that may be tested through the study of specific pulsar properties, as well as general relativistic effects

A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. We have also successfully applied this primary result to demonstrate the nonexistence of certain types of manifolds with specific geometric properties. Specifically, this has enabled us to prove the inexistence of a particular class of manifolds with constant scalar curvature and negative Euler characteristic, thereby overcoming an earlier constraint imposed by a different growth estimate. This inexistence result also extends to certain types of manifolds with compact boundary. Additionally, we have derived an alternative proof of an existing result concerning the compactness of another type of manifolds. This research has been presented in two main sections, with the first section providing the necessary background information and the second section presenting the key results and their applications. This section can be read as a self-contained article. We have also included an appendix as a service to the community. This appendix provides an alternative approach to establishing an estimate concerning the growth of harmonic functions on manifolds with compact boundary, as well as offering a different proof of the results concerning the compactness of a particular type of manifolds. High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, we studied the effects of varying $\gamma$ on parallax measurements from a mission like Gaia, both mathematically and computationally. Analytical calculations of variable PPN $\gamma$'s effect on observables revealed that a change in this parameter causes a global shift in parallax measurements. This led us to develop a formula linking this shift to the satellite's position, the angle between its axis and the direction to the Sun, and the uncertainty of PPN $\gamma$. Computational simulations validated our theoretical predictions. Given current $\gamma$ estimates, we believe its impact on the Gaia parallax measurement zero point is likely minimal, under 0.2 microarcseconds. Additionally, we found that this effect varies significantly with ecliptic latitude, primarily due to the Gaia scanning pattern's asymmetry, supported by additional simulations inverting the direction of the spin axis' precession. This confirms that any distribution of the Gaia satellite's orientation would produce a similar result. Finally, we suggest that future missions similar to Gaia, with similar scanning patterns and orbital characteristics, may experience a $\gamma$-induced zero point shift of a few tenths of a microarcsecond. This effect could potentially be mitigated by adjusting the spin axis' orientation to minimize the satellite's altitude above the ecliptic plane. This, in turn, could further improve parallax measurements and facilitate more precise calculations of the PPN $\gamma$ parameter. This research was conducted as part of the Gaia Inverse Problem Working Group activities.

To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. Furthermore, the approach is extendable to other open-domain question answering tasks that involve accessing vast amounts of information. The code for this approach is available at https://github.com/ghrua/Coarse-to-Careful.

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. The proposed method is further extended to heterogeneous data sets for an additional random walk, and experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the method. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research focuses on offenders who were sentenced to probation and assesses those who were required to undergo mental health treatment against those who were not.  It discovered that receiving mental health treatment as part of their sentence lowered the odds of recidivism within a three-year time frame by 17 percent or 5.6 percentage points.  The data suggests mental health treatment reduces future violent and property crimes more significantly and that this reduction in crimes increases with time since the original conviction.  An initial financial analysis of these results indicates the decrease in future crime could cover and exceed the expenses associated with providing treatment.  A crucial aspect missing from this research is an assessment of why some offenders were ordered to receive mental health treatment versus no treatment, which could impact the results.  A novel approach is used to address this issue by viewing it as an selection bias that is accounted for by incorporating the relevant information into the measurement of the treatment effect.  This approach yields comparable results, which are also analyzed in the paper.  Ultimately, the findings suggest court-ordered mental health treatment reduces future crimes and recidivism within the justice system.  One possible method to interpret the results is to view them as indicating that mental health treatment works, or to view them through a lens of selection, which suggests certain offenders are more likely to be ordered to receive treatment and have lower future crime rates anyway.  The research ends by highlighting the need for more rigorous controls as well as natural experiments that could provide even more accurate results.  A more extensive analysis of future crimes and the time frame in which they occur as well as an analysis of the costs and savings associated with court-ordered mental health treatment is also presented in the paper.  One interesting finding worth noting is that offenders who were ordered to receive treatment had a 10 percentage point higher rate of future crimes that occurred more than two years after the original conviction versus those who were not ordered to receive treatment.  Possible explanations for this finding are discussed in the paper, including the possibility that it is an artifact of the methodology used to measure the duration of future crimes. Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a comprehensive Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates a unified data preprocessing protocol across 7 diverse datasets and integrates 10 leading deep learning knowledge tracing model implementations, enabling transparent and reproducible experiments. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of performance inflation caused by label leakage in certain evaluation settings, and the limited improvement achieved by several deep learning knowledge tracing models when compared to the initial approach proposed by Piech et al. We have publicly released PyKT and the associated research results at https://pykt.org/. We invite researchers and practitioners to collaborate with us and contribute to the advancement of deep learning knowledge tracing. We also provide a straightforward guide to conducting experiments on PyKT in the Appendix section. Given the limited scope of model selection, our research focuses solely on general knowledge tracing, without accommodating customized datasets used in other domains. We believe that PyKT's standardization framework and methodologies will benefit other educational knowledge tracing datasets and domains. Lastly, we emphasize the critical role of rigorous and reproducible experiments in validating deep learning knowledge tracing models, and encourage our peers to engage in this practice. Our results on 7 diverse datasets are available at https://pykt.org/results/NIPS2019_KT_Benchmark. We sincerely hope that PyKT and these results will contribute to the development of more accurate and generalized deep learning knowledge tracing models. Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition. Specifically, it is shown that if a manifold $M$ lacks compact components, then hypersurface gradients are in fact spanned by the range of any second-order elliptic operator $P$ acting on $C^\infty(M)$. This implies that hypersurface gradients can be expressed as the image under a linear operator of $C^\infty(M)$, thereby validating the principle of extension of range, and confirming a prior result of Kopp. Furthermore, this is utilized to derive the confirmation of a prior conjecture of Scheven, whereby it is established that $C^\infty(M)$ can be equivalently identified with the domain of a specific second-order elliptic operator $P$ acting on distributions, provided that the manifold $M$ does not contain any compact components. This is also shown to result in the determination that distributions tangent to the boundary of a manifold without any compact components are inherently smooth. As the number of devices contributing to cross-device federated learning grows, synchronizing updates can significantly reduce efficiency. The FedBuff algorithm mitigates this limitation by enabling asynchronous updates and securely aggregated data sharing, thus improving scalability while protecting user privacy. Building on the FedBuff framework for asynchronous learning, this study enhances existing research by relaxing the requirement that the gradient magnitude must remain within predefined bounds. Theoretical convergence rate analysis of the modified FedBuff algorithm considers factors like diverse data sets, varying batch sizes, and delay intervals. The results show that the modified algorithm preserves the convergence properties of its asynchronous and batch versions while introducing a new parameter that affects the convergence rate. Furthermore, the research includes an updated condition for stagnation avoidance and an expression for the convergence rate when the delay intervals are uniform. The modified FedBuff algorithm and its variants have been successfully tested on real-world data sets, demonstrating improved efficiency and convergence in various scenarios. The research highlights the importance of properly selecting hyperparameters to ensure convergence in both uniform and non-uniform delay settings. The proposed algorithm provides a more adaptable FedBuff framework that can be an efficient solution for large-scale cross-device federated learning. The study concludes by discussing potential modifications and exploring an associated challenge of dynamic model selection. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). Our optimal model achieved a 14% WER reduction on the NuSeD dataset. We also successfully implemented this method on other languages including Slovenian and Bulgarian. Our code has been made available at this link https://github.com/tomkren/ctf_cz_en.

Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and with minimal modifications, this variant is obtainable. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. The proposed method also achieves a 0.75 F score on average when compared to conventional tuning with 80% of the test data. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/ghrua/FewShotGEC.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, through our investigation, we also established the existence of a mechanism with two agents that, for any possible values, always has pure Nash equilibria inducing allocations that are fair up to any good with respect to their underlying values, without violating honesty or value-Truthfulness. This latter property enables us to characterise allocations that are fair up to any good as those that, for any possible values, always have pure Nash equilibria inducing them in a fair allocation setting.
