UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. The anomalous behavior of its stars also suggests that UGC 8839 may be the result of a past major merger with a massive gas-poor galaxy. The extensive study of UGC 8839 includes a 3D dynamical modeling of its rotation curve, a comparison with $H{\alpha}$ luminosity distributions in other galaxies, a comprehensive visual and spectral analysis, and an examination of its stellar and gas components through a radiative transfer model of its light and radiative transfer simulations of its HII regions. The resulting 3D model reveals a distinct, rapidly rotating inner disk and a vast, slowly rotating outer disk dominated by dark matter. The extensive research on UGC 8839 has implications for the various mechanisms that regulate its star formation, including its unique massive HII region, and the different models that predict its behavior, including a low-level activity nuclear star cluster. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide a rare, illustrative example of an exceptionally stable galaxy disk that thrives in an isolated environment, in contrast to an environment characterized by strong tidal interactions and a supermassive central black hole. The extensive data collected on UGC 8839 includes a comprehensive catalog of its stellar and gas components, along with a 3D rotation curve, a 3D distribution of its HII regions, a comprehensive visual and spectral analysis, and various models of its behavior and structure. Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Our code is available at https://github.com/AI-Education/Offline-Multi-Agent-RL.

We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. Furthermore, we applied this network to align 2D brain images with their corresponding kV images using attenuation maps, facilitating dose calculation during radiation therapy. Additionally, 3D registrations were performed to analyze capture range and local contrast enhancement methods to expand the network's capture range while preserving local image features. Comparisons with conventional methods revealed a superior Dice coefficient in all cases. The proposed network was then utilized to align 3D brain images with megavoltage images, resulting in a 63.6% success rate according to the PLCC metric. The code is available online at: https://github.com/ghasemipoursohi/MV-Image-Registration.

In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Furthermore, we highlight the inadequacy of averaging the degree of steering across an ensemble of single-particle states, as it significantly distorts the genuine non-local phenomenon resulting from single-particle entanglement. In such a scenario, a proper measure of the averaged degree of influence that can be exerted on the particle's wave function following measurement by the influencing party is proposed. This is found to be directly proportional to the squared difference between the wave functions corresponding to different detectors used by the influencing party. V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail.  Post eruption spectra showed both a persistent narrow-line spectrum of the accretion disk as well as the fading of the ejected particles, which were illuminated by an intense ongoing X-ray emission.  Optical data reveal an orbital period of nearly three and a half days while the absence of the white dwarf spin frequency presents further evidence for a massive WD.  The pre and post nova energy distributions also indicate a massive accretion rate.  V392 Persei, unlike many novae and dwarf novae systems, did not switch to its initial low mass transfer configuration, but instead stayed in its high mass transfer state, which we believe is as a result of the irradiation of the companion by the massive nova explosion, thus it exhibits a level of similarity with another renowned system known as GK Persei.  The extensive electron capture of 12C by oxygen rich matter at both normal and massive densities also became apparent during the observation period, which presents another distinguishing feature for this system.  The extensive observations of V392 Persei also present a unique theoretical challenge, which could also offer valuable insights about other deeply observed objects such as the famous classical nova known as Nova Delphi 2016.

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Numerical evaluation confirms the system's effectiveness across different scenarios. Moreover, by reducing data transfer between base station and mobile terminal, the GMM-based approach facilitates easier deployment and management of massive machine-type communications. The proposed method's performance is comparable to that of traditional approaches in scenarios with ample feedback data transmission. The codebook and GMM can be configured to trade-off feedback data transfer and system performance. The proposed method's applicability has been demonstrated across various frequencies, with results showing achievable rate gains of up to 30% over traditional approaches. The codebase has been made available online. The proposed feedback encoding algorithm can be combined with or adapted from existing transceiver designs, enabling the integration of learning-based codebook construction in FDD systems. The codebase includes examples of combined designs with existing transceivers, including massivimTC and large-scale antenna systems, along with simulation results confirming the feasibility and effectiveness of these combinations. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These findings suggest that the most massive of these remnants may prefer specific galaxy environments that are distinct from those preferred by lower mass binaries. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. 
To demonstrate the potential of TextWorldExpress, we established three challenging levels of evaluation for interested developers, consisting of increased time constraints that reflect real-world benchmarks. 
By pushing the speed of text-based games to unprecedented levels, we believe TextWorldExpress will serve as a crucial tool for evaluating virtual agents requiring high performance in tasks involving rapid interaction with complex environments. 
The framework is highly modular, easily extendable, and compatible with a range of assessment frameworks used today. 
It can be accessed at https://textworldexpress.org.

Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated design of algorithms and hardware to achieve high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the self-repulsive properties of a specific particle in long-range interactions. A new, closely related formulation suggests it could be formulated in terms of a particle's self-binding energy, which must remain non-negative. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The novelty of this formulation's structure allows it to bypass any allusion to the theory's holographic duality and spacetime locality. Consequently, it's hypothesized that the property of a convex spectrum of charges should apply broadly to all conformal field theories that are unitary. Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. However, this condition does not hold without further constraints, as evident from constructed examples. Based on the ring's properties and test elements, we find formulas to compute various coefficients, which are in turn used to establish the relationship between $F$-rationality and these coefficients, ultimately leading to the condition for $F$-rationality as depth $R \geq 2$ and a specific equality of these coefficients. This equality does not guarantee $F$-rationality for rings with a ring dimension equal to $2$, as demonstrated by counterexamples. On the other hand, we demonstrate that rings with a ring dimension equal to $2$ are $F$-rational when they have depth $R \geq 3$ and a specific prime characteristic. This implies that depth $R \geq 3$ is a necessary and sufficient condition for those rings to be $F$-rational. This conclusion generalizes the result from Huneke and Swanson for rings with a specific ring dimension and without a parameter. Lastly, we establish that the condition of depth $R \geq 2$ can be relaxed to a certain condition based on the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, which in turn can be further relaxed to a different condition, ultimately leading to the definition of a specific ring as excellent local $F$-rational, which serves as the key result of this paper. This key result enables us to generalize the result from Huneke and Swanson for rings with a specific ring dimension and without a parameter to rings with any ring dimension and with a parameter, provided that they are excellent local $F$-rational. This paper also includes an additional result which can be considered as a special case of a more general statement, known as the weak implication of the direct method

The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. The model facilitates a deeper examination of these issues and provides actionable policy advice through the design of suitable agent incentives and market parameters. The model has been successfully applied to evaluate a multi-agent order type redispatch market, which yields novel performance indicators and encourages further investigation into design options. The results highlight the complexities of electricity markets and the challenges of translating theoretical concepts into practical policy advice. A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of a certain vertex coloring in a transformed version of the graph. This notion was initially proposed as an open problem by Faudree, Schelp, Gyárfás, and Tuza in 1990, assuming a bipartite graph of high enough girth and a specific degree constraint could be colored using a certain number of colors, but in 2021 this was contested. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. Our model and associated data are available at: https://github.com/ghrua/MCSCL.

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. By introducing a new model featuring migration channels and testing it using Santiago's data, our results reveal that incorporating discrete migration channels, rather than continuous diffusion, is crucial for modeling the city's rioting distribution. Furthermore, by analyzing the model's parameters, we found that a critical threshold exists, beyond which increased mobility among the infected population ultimately leads to the disorder's acceleration, in contrast to slower acceleration observed when this barrier is not surpassed. In addition to these findings, we found that the model's ability to replicate the observed temporal patterns is compromised when it fails to account for changes in population dynamics during specific time periods. A notable feature of this model is its capability to derive mathematical expressions from empirical data, achieved by approximating the model's parameters using the rioting distribution's moments. This led to an alternative, non-epidemiological representation of the disorders' dynamics, presented in the form of a non-local fractional differential equation. This equation's properties were then analyzed, revealing its connection to the original epidemiological model, and demonstrating its effectiveness in capturing the disorders' temporal and spatial patterns with reasonable accuracy. A key aspect of this model is its ability to incorporate the effects of population displacement by including the fraction index in the differential equation, which can be determined using the distribution of unrest. In conclusion, this project's findings suggest that the epidemiological model's failure to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago during the 2019 riots can be attributed to the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement, which is essential for capturing the city's rioting patterns. In contrast, the model's ability to account for changes in population dynamics during specific time periods is reflected in the time-dependent fraction index, which must be determined using empirical data for an accurate representation of the disorders' dynamics. In addition to its applications in epidemiology and sociology, this model has the potential to be adapted for modeling other complex phenomena, which can be influenced by the distribution of resources, population displacement, and changes in population

This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. We also explore the application of our method to regular expressions over finite character sets and prove that it yields a decidable problem. Moreover, we investigate the containment problem within a specific subset of regular expressions, demonstrating that it is computationally hard and collectively undecidable, along with an extension of this result to context-free languages. We conclude by examining the relationship between our method and conventional approaches, including the use of finite state automata, monadic second-order logic, and Brzozowski's derivative operator, as well as exploring potential connections to other problems and themes. Alongside this, we provide a related but distinct idea of solving context-free system inequalities. The proposed algorithm has been implemented in the REWIG solver, which is now part of the public SMTLIB standard, and we include an evaluation of the solver based on a previously established benchmark. Lastly, we outline possible future research paths, including an examination of the solver's output for additional insights, an exploration of the solver's effectiveness with finite character sets, and an investigation of the containment problem within specific context-free languages.

Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. The proposed method's superiority is also proven by showing that it outperforms current and classical VIO models in various difficult scenarios, such as indoor environments with substantial light variations and outdoor environments with rolling shutter effect. The proposed model's efficiency and efficacy are also reflected in its low pose estimation cost, which is observable in the experimental results. The code for the proposed model is available online at https://github.com/Shoukai-Huang/EMA-VIO.

This paper introduces the Federated Selective Aggregation (FedSA) challenge, a novel approach that allows the creation of a student model for a specific task by incorporating information from multiple unconnected teachers who have trained on various projects. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. The resulting code is available at https://github.com/ChengzeLiu/FedSA.

We investigate the minimal time it takes for a qubit state to evolve from an initial state into a distinguishable state under both unitary and non-unitary dynamics. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. For non-unitary dynamics, we compare several bounds on distinguishability time, including a novel lower bound related to the system-environment asymmetry and expressed in terms of a specific matrix norm. Finally, we discuss the connection between asymmetry, entanglement, and the Haar measure on the Bloch ball, which contributes to a deeper understanding of the dynamics of a specific open system. These findings enrich our understanding of the minimal time required to release a qubit system and the associated speed limits. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. Additionally, we analyze the impact of substrate choice and carrier concentration on resonator decay rates and quantum volume. This research highlights the significance of terahertz investigations in evaluating and developing quantum devices, and demonstrates the effectiveness of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. This includes a discussion of transfer embedding and the related protocol of vector calibration. This study was conducted at the terahertz near-field microscopy facility at Yale University. This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. Last, we examine the implications of this knowledge for Earth and other exoplanets. This work is an invitation to the scientific community to engage with the challenging and fascinating case of Venus, with the goal of expanding our understanding of this planet's complex and dynamic atmosphere through collaborative research. Ultimately, this knowledge will also contribute to a deeper comprehension of Earth's evolution and the mechanisms that have kept our planet habitable. This research has important implications for the search for life on planets with similar atmosphere compositions, as it highlights the significance of atmospheric escape in shaping a planet's evolution and highlights the risk of exoplanetary environments that may appear habitable at first glance but are actually subject to extreme conditions. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. The proposed MuLE concept can also be applied to other types of optics, such as micro-channel plate (MCP) X-ray optics. The MuLE arrangement outperforms a conventional LE configuration even when considering the additional time spent on re-constructing the image, and it achieves this improvement with a factor of 10 times greater in sensitivity. The proposed concept of MuLE optics can be implemented in various configurations, and we present several ideas, including one involving a single LE mirror combined with a pyramid mirror array. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. These simulations took the initial state of a rotating star, calculated its evolution over time, and compared the results to observational data from companion stars in the X-ray binary 4U 1538-52, finding that the method accurately replicates these phenomena. 

Furthermore, our method has been applied to neutron stars, hypermassive neutron stars, and carbon-oxygen white dwarfs, among other objects, and has been found to converge with existing theoretical predictions, offering a promising alternative for studying the evolution of rotating stars.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Furthermore, our findings indicate that selective labeling coupled with active learning on rich data formats like PDFs can achieve the same level of performance as traditional labeling methods, using datasets that have been partially annotated in simple text formats like CSVs. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. The network's effectiveness is showcased in its capacity to differentiate between all types of merging compact binaries, distinguishing them from background noise. With approximately 500,000 training samples, we successfully trained a network that can recover known neutron star and binary neutron star events, and accurately classify a vast majority of candidate black hole binary merger events. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. We also explore a method to predict electromagnetic emissions associated with neutron star and black hole mergers, using the trained network to recover key event characteristics from gravitational waves, and matching observed electromagnetic radiation with theoretical models of electromagnetic emissions induced by mergers. Ultimately, this research paves the way for efficiently detecting and analyzing all types of merging compact binaries, and provides a crucial step towards predicting electromagnetic emissions associated with these events. We make our code available to the public, hoping it will facilitate similar deep learning applications in multi-messenger astronomy. Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for managing public health policies in a way that balances strict measures with promoting diversity of urban encounters beyond the pandemic era. Moreover, this study highlights the significance of considering the complex interplay between individual behaviors, group dynamics, and community resilience in urban diversity, which is vital for informing policy decisions that prioritize both public health and diversity in urban environments. Lastly, adapting to new normal conditions could be achieved by implementing targeted interventions that address changed preferences and habits, fostering innovative approaches to valorizing the economic benefits derived from diverse urban interactions. The study also utilizes a novel, simple model of probability distributions that captures the dynamics of urban diversity, providing actionable insights for policymakers, businesses, and community leaders, and offering a valuable tool for forecasting the future of urban diversity, subject to changing individual behaviors and public health policies. The model used in this study can be applied to other contexts where probability distributions and their dynamics are crucial, such as analyzing income inequalities within populations or assessing the diversity of innovative startups. Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields stable and secure indoor navigation in the presence of moving objects. Alternatively, when sensors are blocked or unable to operate, the system can adapt to provide reliable data for route planning through the remaining sensors. Furthermore, this research provides a foundation for extending navigation to three-dimensional indoor environments using sonar sensors. Experimental data was obtained from real-time testing on a mobile robot within a office environment, using one to three sonar sensors, and is available at: http://www.sciencedirect.com/.

The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. Social media has fueled the spread of misinformation by offering convenient access, coupled with limited fact-checking mechanisms. Given the negative consequences of this type of information on society, pinpointing false news has become increasingly vital. We propose an innovative method that leverages transformer-based language models to counter one of their inherent drawbacks, allowing our CMTR-BERT framework to combine diverse text representations, mitigate the sequential constraints inherent to the underlying architecture, and integrate contextual information effectively. Experimental evaluations using two disparate, publicly available datasets showcase our method's capability to achieve superior performance benchmarks, highlighting the benefits of both utilizing automatic text summarization and incorporating contextual information for enhanced performance. Moreover, our findings highlight potential areas for improvement in the underlying architecture of large pre-trained language models, paving the way for further exploration in related research communities. We also present a straightforward, real-world application of our framework, demonstrating its practical utility in fake news detection contexts. This involves training a binary classifier using summary-based features, which yields an 8% improvement in F1-score compared to the current state-of-the-art baseline. We also explore a related problem known as online false news detection, which relies on automatic text summarization to excel, resulting in an 11% improvement in F1-score. We make our code available at https://github.com/abhishek6499/CMTR-BERT.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these systems – the geometry of their parametric space – using statistical tools to simulate and model the systems' dynamics. The results revealed an intriguing phenomenon dubbed the "curvature effect," where a significant increase in a system's disorder is associated with an irregular geometric change, linked to the emergence of an internal timeline that influences the systems' progression over time. The study also pares down its mathematical representations to minimize complexity and recasts the models using a simpler random field framework, which allows for an in-depth analysis of the curvature effect and its associated time-based implications. The findings have been validated through multiple simulations and a comparative study of the models, which showed that the curvature effect's impact can vary significantly depending on the systems' underlying assumptions and parameters. Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels. To validate our method, we fine-tune BERT on a limited subset of EMO20Q, thereby establishing a standard against which our approach's effectiveness is measured. We find that our method succeeds in refining the annotations of a subset of EMO20Q, albeit with room for improvement in enhancing simple labels and expanding to other annotated data sets. Finally, we explore a more straightforward evaluation of BERT that hinges on the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases, and experiment with incorporating both BERT-based evaluation methods into the annotation process by means of a semi-supervised transcription game, the results of which indicate that players' annotations are predominantly corrected in line with the BERT-assisted annotations. We make available the annotated and annotated/played data sets at: \url{http://www.emo20q.org/annotation.html}.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. This achievement could also pave the way for detecting leaky local magnetic fields generated by quantum systems, such as ferromagnetic atomic clouds, at the level of individual atoms. Moreover, this approach could be adapted to measure magnetic properties of materials at the atomic level, and it offers a novel method for implementing atomic sensing of the surrounding environment. The technical feasibility of this idea has been demonstrated through a working demonstration of atomic interferometry in a setup that measures the change in the local magnetic field caused by a change in superconducting state, achieving a precision of $10^{-13}$ Tesla. The inherent scalability of this setup, which can be expanded to multiple atomic layers, suggests it can be adapted to investigate the relationship between superconducting materials' magnetic properties and atomic structure, although this would require more sophisticated data analysis involving quantum fluids' hydrodynamic theory. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  As additional proof of its effectiveness, DynaSOAr's memory allocator alone was found to yield better results than leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by achieving a 5 times speedup and a 2 times size support increase in separate memory allocation and memory allocation without execution benchmark tests.  In summary, the DynaSOAr framework provides an easy-to-adapt-to environment for GPU programming by overcoming memory allocation and access inefficiencies, offering a simple and intuitive memory layout DSL, a lock-free and parallel memory allocator, and efficient execution and memory management through combined allocation and execution atomic operations.  Consequently, DynaSOAr facilitates high-speed GPU programming for a previously overlooked category of object-oriented applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures.  The framework's memory allocator and layout DSL are general-purpose and compatible with a range of programming languages, including C++, Fortran, and Java, whereas its do-all operation is specifically optimized for CUDA and OpenACC.  As open-source software, DynaSOAr is available for download via GitHub.  In our benchmark tests, DynaSOAr demonstrated a 3 times speedup and a 2 times size support increase in SMMO application code performance

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations of Mn adatoms and Mn dimers on the Nb(110) surface were conducted and the results compared with experimental data. In the case of the isolated Mn adatom, slight spin-orbit coupling effects were observed, while localized spin polarization on Nb atoms showed marginal influence. Additionally, by scaling the exchange field, the absence of a $d_{x^2-y^2}$-like YSR state in the spectrum was explained. For a close-packed ferromagnetic dimer, satisfactory agreement with experimental results regarding YSR state splitting was found. However, for an antiferromagnetic dimer, spin-orbit coupling was insufficient to account for observed state splitting. Reversal of the magnetic dimer's moment alignment led to YSR state splitting, along with a notable shift in energy and formation of a zero-bias peak for the most deeply seated YSR state. This outcome can be understood as resulting from the interplay of exchange interaction, spin-orbit coupling, and the dimer's alignment, and may have implications for understanding YSR states in other magnetic configurations. This theoretical framework has been applied to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities on the Nb(110) surface, and has highlighted the complexity of YSR states and the necessity of precise analysis in order to accurately interpret experimental data.

The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the detection of rarest transiting planetary systems. In a new discovery, we found a young star called TOI-712, hosting a system of four planets orbiting it. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an age ranging from approximately $500$ million to 1.1 billion years. Observations from $TESS$ revealed three mini-Neptune-sized planets with distinct periods of $9.531$ days, $51.699$ days, and $84.839$ days. Additionally, the team detected an Earth-sized candidate called TOI-712.05 with a short orbital period of $4.32$ days. By calculating the habitable zone for this system, TOI-712 d appears to lie on the inner boundary, and further research into TOI-712, with a brightness of $9.9$, is worthwhile due to its relatively young and temperate conditions. Despite initial assessments, follow-up spectroscopic analyses classified TOI-712 as a giant star instead of a sub-giant, leading to an estimated mass of $2.5$ solar masses and a luminescence of $4.5$ solar luminosities. Consequently, the outer boundary of the habitable zone now lies just $500,000$ miles beyond the TOI-712 d orbit and TOI-712's large size may have a significant impact on its planetary retention, making it an unlikely haven for life. Furthermore, the system's orientation, with an inclination of about $45$ degrees, results in the planets' orbits crossing each other's paths, leading to possible tidal interactions and the potential for internal heating. These factors, in combination with the lack of spectral lines from TOI-712's atmosphere, make it an intriguing target for future studies, such as observing the star's rotation, analyzing the planets' compositions, and searching for additional planetary bodies within the system.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2.  To accurately simulate these properties, we utilized a 48-atom supercell through the VASP code, relaxing both atomic positions and cell dimensions to minimize errors. The results indicate that substitutional carbon and nitrogen defects have a tendency for anti-ferromagnetic long-range ordering with corresponding magnetic moments of 2$\mu B$ and 1$\mu B$ for carbon and nitrogen respectively.  Conversely, nitrogen defects positioned interstitially possess a fixed magnetic moment of 1$\mu B$ whereas carbon defects positioned interstitially display no magnetism.  Moreover, calculations demonstrate that interstitial N defects lie at a saddle point in the total energy landscape, and that a more stable configuration is reached when these atoms bond with oxygen in a CO or NO dimer.  Notably, this outcome is consistent with earlier experimental findings utilizing XPS that also identified such N-O bonds, and could potentially be verified via spectroscopic techniques.  Moreover, both doped carbon and nitrogen defects reside within the band gap of TiO2.  We propose that tuning TiO2 by introducing such defects could enhance its photocatalytic properties.  Lastly, our findings also highlight the necessity for accurate supercell size and structural relaxation on magnetic and electronic properties.  We further investigated the effects of different exchange-correlation functionals and found that some, such as PBE, overestimate the magnetic moments achieved by both carbon and nitrogen defects.  We propose a new approach that involves averaging the magnetic moment over neighboring Ti and O atoms to overcome this limitation, and demonstrate this method's applicability to other transition metal oxides.  Lastly, we explored the effects of different dopant locations and found that both carbon and nitrogen exhibit similar behavior when placed within the Ti or O sublattices respectively.  We also found that moving the N defect from a substitutional to interstitial position involves a phase transition that occurs when the distance between N and its nearest neighbor Ti or O reaches a certain threshold, and that this distance varies depending on the functional used to calculate it.  We propose that this behavior could be general to other transition metal oxides and other d-block elements. This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively. Additionally, I discuss the potential discovery of the semi-elastic process at the Large Hadron Collider's higher energy setting of 13 TeV, which could reveal the absolute cross-section of the semi-elastic process, as well as other rare decays, and demonstrate that the inclusion of additional triggers can significantly broaden the range of possible rare decays that can be detected. Lastly, I outline the requirements for realizing these possibilities with the existing detector infrastructure and the opportunities that arise with the development of a highly luminous, upgraded version of the Large Hadron Collider.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits. Moreover, our study identifies potential optimal qudit sizes that balance computational resources with precision, and demonstrates that, in theory, qutrits hold theoretical advantages over qubits in simulated landspaces, ending with a comment on the necessity of exploring noise simulations in realistic quantum simulation scenarios. Lastly, we offer a practical application of our analysis to a variational quantum algorithms implementation of sQED. For this, we propose a realistic simulation strategy on a qutrit-based variational quantum simulator, specifically the Gaussian Quantum Neural Network, and demonstrate how defining an appropriate gauge can reduce landspace noise effects to a negligible level. Alternatively, without defining a gauge, our findings show that noise's minimal impact occurs when the number of variational parameters per qudit is equal to the qudit size itself. A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for the effects of temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to thoroughly explore this finding's effect on the established correlation between the mass function of prestellar cores and the mass function of the newly formed stars.  It's also crucial to examine the role of core growth in facilitating the formation of massive stars, as well as to investigate the timescales involved in this process.  Finally, we discuss the similarities between the Dragon infrared dark cloud and the Cygnus X complex, both observed in the far-infrared and the millimeter regime, and highlight the distinct core mass functions present in each location.  The absence of massive prestellar cores in the Dragon infrared dark cloud is particularly notable, with its protostellar and starless cores exhibiting a mass ratio of approximately 5:1.  This ratio is distinct from the typical mass function of prestellar cores, which demonstrates a maximum mass of approximately 30 solar masses.  The possible relationship between core gas surface density and the appearance of molecular outflows is also explored, with outflows observed in cores with average gas surface densities exceeding 10 times the minimum required for self-gravity.  The presence of outflows in these high-density cores is inconsistent with the established view that outflows necessarily clear dense gas and dust.  Instead, it's possible that outflows are instead associated with the growth of these dense cores, with outflows and core growth exhibiting a cyclical relationship.  The millimeter core mass functions of both the Dragon infrared dark cloud and the Cygnus X complex demonstrate a steady decline in core mass distribution, with 80% of cores possessing masses below 10 solar masses.  The presence of massive starless cores is absent in both locations, with the ground-based limit of detectability currently set at 20 solar masses.  Further research is necessary to fully account for the effects of beam smoothing, background emission, and the influence of massive star formation within the Cygnus X complex, specifically in its central regions

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available. This achieved a plasma density of approximately 4 x 10^10 per cubic centimeter in a 0.02 meter long plasma column. Further improvements showed it was possible to extend plasma density to 1.5 x 10^11 per cubic centimeter in a 0.1 meter long plasma column, demonstrating the effectiveness of IShTAR's plasma source. It has since been used to investigate how radio frequency waves affect plasma, as well as being adapted for other applications involving plasma etching. The source's versatility makes it suitable for a broad range of experiments, including those involving etching and chemical vapor deposition. The findings from IShTAR have significant value for other similar facilities around the world, and the source's design can be applied to them, even though they often have different scales and purposes. The development of the IShTAR source also sparked interest in a related concept known as the helicon double plasma, which could provide an even more efficient way of producing plasma. The facility has since been upgraded to investigate this further, and it has led to the discovery of a previously unknown phenomenon involving how plasma interacts with the helical antenna, and how it affects particle power balance and plasma parameters. The knowledge gained from the IShTAR facility has significant implications for a range of applications, and it has the potential to contribute significantly to the development of future facilities, even though it is an experimental device rather than a commercial product. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. Moreover, this methodology enables researchers to explore the role of overfitting in point annotation-based models, revealing that models prone to overfitting tend to perform poorly in density masks prediction. The proposed W-shaped network achieves superior performance in detecting nuclei in pathology images, as demonstrated by both point annotation-based and density mask evaluation methods. Compared to existing models, at 10% threshold, the model's average F-score for predicting density masks is 0.78, and for point annotation masks is 0.91. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/ghrasoul/W-Net. The model has also been tested on separate datasets, with results showing it can be adapted for other tasks, such as lymphocyte detection. The documentation for this project, along with code for training and evaluating the model, is available at https://github.com/ghrasoul/W-Net-doc. The documentation includes a detailed explanation of the model's methodology, as well as guidelines for modifying it to suit other purposes. The model has been integrated into an application for automatically segmenting images, available at https://github.com/ghrasoul/W-Net-application. Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F) respectively. This paper focuses on establishing the local converse theorem for the representation of G. To this end, for two given irreducible admissible generic representations of G, with shared central character and gamma factors, our result stipulates that these representations are isomorphic. To prove this, we draw from the Cogdell, Shahidi, and Tsai framework of partial Bessel functions and the categorization of irreducible generic representations. Furthermore, our result extends the earlier works by Jiang and Soudry as well as Q. Zhang, by expanding on their results for the cases with supercuspidal representations in a wider set of characteristic settings. Additionally, our result demonstrates the applicability of the local converse theorem to certain cases involving certain types of classical groups in a characteristic setting, which was previously unexamined. Moreover, our methodical approach allows for the derivation of the isomorphism class of the representation Sp(2r+2)(F) for any r>0, which was initially proposed by L. L. Yang. Lastly, our result can be specifically realized for the particular setting with r=1, which was specifically examined by G. L. T. H. Jackson.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. A software implementation of GCNNs using matched filtering principles is also developed and put to the test on real-world datasets, against established benchmarks, with results showing minimal performance differences. This work aims to enhance the intuitive grasp of GCNNs, encouraging further exploration of matched filtering in AI, and providing a platform for custom GCNN developments. A code repository associated with this research is available at https://github.com/ahmadow/matchfilter-gcnn.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. We also achieve this storage capability while ensuring that our solution's accuracy remains within a factor of at most $O(\min\{\sqrt{\Delta}\cdot \lambda_d(N)\cdot \Delta^{\frac{1}{3}} + 1\})$ relative to an optimal $k$-means clustering for the final data stream. Furthermore, our algorithm incorporates an efficient update procedure that allows for seamless integration into various existing coreset recovery schemes, thereby enabling a broad range of applications including, but not limited to, scattering-based coreset recovery, Fourier domain analysis, and streaming clustering via multiple passes over the data. We also provide a more comprehensive discussion on the interconnection between our algorithm and these reference solutions, offering a specialized case where our algorithm's performance excels in comparison to these reference solutions. We complement our single-pass solution with a parametrized analysis of a previous one-pass algorithm proposed by [Bubey, Kanade, and Sharma], which reveals that the aforementioned previous algorithm is equivalent to a variant of our single-pass solution for the case where the minimum distance $\lambda_d(N)$ between any two points within the dataset is sufficiently large, i.e., greater than the cube root of $\Delta$. We also provide a theoretical lower bound on the storage capacity of any one-pass algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem, which serves as a theoretical storage capacity lower bound for our single-pass solution as well. We developed our solution using a novel technique that involves combining the scattering transform with the Fourier domain analysis, and also showed that this solution can be applied to a broad range of high-dimensional data clustering tasks, which include, but are not limited to, streaming clustering via multiple passes over the data, and provided a special case analysis where our solution outperforms existing references solutions. We believe that our solution and the associated technique provide valuable insights for both the machine learning and signal processing communities, which may also be extended to other high-dimensional data clustering tasks beyond the $k$-means clustering problem. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. Moreover, it enables a meaningful analysis of the grilled world architecture, unveiling insights into the grid structure's impact on gameplay. We validate our model across a range of scenarios, including dynamically generated and uncertain grids, showing that it excels in situations involving large grids and narrow corridors. Our hierarchical model also yields a notable performance boost when implemented on a specific real-world domain. We outline a range of future research possibilities arising from this work. The associated code is publicly available at https://github.com/AndreasKessler/HierarchicalPursuitEvasion.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. A key contribution of this study involves the public integration of Effective W/Z and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations, collectively referred to as the Effective Vector Boson Approximation, into the existing event generator software MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO, setting the groundwork for developing matching prescriptions between EW parton showers and EW distribution functions, and providing actionable advice on the use of W/Z PDFs to facilitate this development. A comprehensive comparison is made between EWA and W/Z PDFs, accompanied by a qualitative analysis of leading order 2-to-n particle interactions facilitated by EWA. A key finding of this study involves the discovery that, at energy levels above a few TeV, the influence of boson collinearity cuts surpasses the impact of boson distribution functions, following a power law with a $\sim 5$ exponent. A crucial aspect of this research involves providing accessible code tools to the high-energy particle physics community, specifically a MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO version that includes EWA and W/Z PDFs, as well as a user-friendly script for generating soft W/Z PDFs. A further analysis is conducted of 2-to-4 particle interactions at 29.7 TeV energy levels, following a 1.2 TeV center-of-mass collision, to validate the EWA method and MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO integration. A key outcome of this analysis involves the discovery that the EWA method successfully reproduces the original results obtained using W/Z PDFs, following a ratio distribution with a $\sim 1$ average and a $\sim 0.2$ standard deviation. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our results demonstrate that isolating networks significantly
improves performance and eliminates task confusion and interference. To further
analze this approach, we also provide a theoretical explanation of why and when
task interference may occur in learned multi-task dynamics models. Our study and
associated code are available at: \url{https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.02063.pdf}.
