In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. By incorporating noise as input to the conditional GAN, we significantly enhanced the quality of sampled images and reduced the gap between trained and actual posterior distribution samples. This was especially evident when evaluating the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the posterior distribution and sampled images. We also introduced a new training objective for conditional WGAN that is both regularized and conditional, which has not been explored before. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. This finding is supported by all previous studies placing the boundaries of the Local Bubble at 5.5 parsecs from the Earth. Alternatively, another screen is linked to a dense object in the line of sight to the pulsar, likely a star, and its velocity matches the motion of the Galactic center, implying that the star lies within the Local Bubble. The remaining screens have more uncertain associations with the surrounding interstellar medium. The accumulation of 134 separate scintillation patterns over the Earth's orbit and the pulsar's rotation enabled the recovery of the pulsar's beam properties, specifically the width of its beam, confirming that it is highly elliptical. The analysis of beam properties and screen associations with the surrounding interstellar medium highlights the complex structure of the line of sight to the pulsar, consisting of multiple screens and a dense object, and highlights the difficulties in interpreting the data using current models of the Local Bubble. The extensive dataset available for the pulsar B1133+16 also offers opportunities for further analysis, such as studying the variability of beam properties, the screening of the pulsar by the Earth, and the distribution of the scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit. The findings presented in this paper are a result of reanalyzing historical Arecibo observations, and the infrastructure developed for this project also enables the analysis of future observations of the pulsar, providing a valuable resource for any future observations of B1133+16. The methods used to analyze the data and the infrastructure developed for this project are relevant to other pulsar observations and can be applied to other pulsars observed under similar conditions. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Code for QPNet is available at: https://github.com/Parandosean/QPNet.git. Human assessments of speech samples generated with QPNet show significant improvements over WN and other baselines in terms of naturalness, with scores of 4.25, 4.03, and 3.63 respectively. Additionally, the MOS scores of WN and QPNet for unseen frequency inputs at a fundamental frequency of 250 Hz are 3.53 and 4.23 respectively, indicating the advantages of QPNet in controlling the pitch of generated signals. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our project features a sound source localization TensorFlow model available online.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. LGCN's simplicity and efficiency make it a valuable tool for various applications involving graph learning in complex, hierarchical structures. The code for LGCN is available at https://github.com/ShuaiNiu/LGCN.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. This inverse problem is ill-posed, and therefore, its solution requires a regularization method. A Tikhonov regularized scheme is proposed and proven to converge to the exact solution, with the error bound depending on the mesh size, data discrepancy, and other factors. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, with the error bounds asymptotically approaching the expected behavior as the mesh size decreases. These experiments are conducted using a finite element method for spatial discretization and a quasi-optimality property of the Tikhonov regularized solution. The Tikhonov regularized scheme's performance is also compared to the iterative regularization scheme, known as the Landweber iteration, with the results indicating that the Tikhonov regularized scheme yields a more accurate and stable solution. When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  This specific gauge choice also results in a linearized massive gravity model when applied to a symmetric traceless tensor field, which has only two degrees of freedom.  We also examine the full nonlinear version of this harmonic gauge, demonstrating that the associated symmetry of the monopole mode is altered and that the specific gauge leads to a massive gravity theory with a quadratic potential for the scalar component, which is then compared to the established literature using a different coordinate convention.  We conclude by discussing potential obstacles to applying this specific harmonic gauge choice to full nonlinear gravity, including the issue of whether it is compatible with the assumption of a static universe.  We also examine the relation with the de Donder gauge and the impact of the assumption of a static universe on the gauge choice.  Furthermore, we derive the specific harmonic gauge choice that arises when a mass term is added to a general covariant gauge, which is then applied to both linearized and full nonlinear gravity, relying on a precise expansion of the harmonic gauge operator.  We also explore the relation with the Bicentennial gauge, which is found to be equivalent to the de Donder gauge within linearized gravity, whereas in the context of full nonlinear gravity the Bicentennial gauge leads to a massive gravity theory with a linear potential for the scalar component.  We conclude by analyzing the specific examples of the harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to both the standard general relativistic gravitational field equations and the Einstein-Hilbert action, relying on a proper expansion of the harmonic gauge operator. The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Additionally, this approach may provide a richer learning experience compared to conventional, purely analytical explanations. A few potential misconceptions about negative temperature are also addressed in the report. Moreover, an affiliated MATLAB code is available for downloading, which allows users to visualize the concept of a two-level system at negative absolute temperature across various scenarios. This report was originally presented as a talk at the Michigean Mathematics and Science Teaching Conference held in Ann Arbor, Michigan in 2019. The conference was organized by the University of Michigan's Physics Department in collaboration with Michigan State University. The report is now being published in the PRST-PER conference series. The associated MATLAB code has been made available for download from the arXiv website. The report consists of the following sections: introduction, theoretical background, negative temperature, two-level systems, quantum computing, and conclusions. The report also includes an appendix on the Bose-Einstein distribution and another appendix on the associated MATLAB code. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Our findings suggest that GAN-based image editing can be both efficient and effective in medical applications. Our code is available at https://github.com/gharsani/DiseaseAwareEditing.
